title: CC CPSU Politburo Session March 17-18, 1979
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Politburo session convened urgently after the Herat uprising, in which Soviet advisers were killed. Nearly all members opposed sending troops, though some argued the USSR could not lose Afghanistan. Brezhnev summed up that economic and military aid and advisers would be provided but no Soviet troops.

title: Transcript of Telephone Conversation Between Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin and Afghan Prime Minister Nur Mohammed Taraki, March 18, 1979
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Kosygin tells Taraki the USSR will not send troops and urges him to rely on the local population, including mobilizing industrial workers in Herat province. This shows Soviet misunderstanding of local conditions. Source: CWIHP Bulletin 8-9, pp. 145-146.

title: Transcript of A. N. Kosygin-A.A. Gromyko-D.F. Ustinov-B.N. Ponomarev-N.M. Taraki Conversation on March 20, 1979
authors: Soviet leadership (Kosygin, Gromyko, Ustinov, Ponomarev) and Nur Mohammed Taraki
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Conversation between Soviet leaders and Taraki during the Herat crisis, when the Afghan leadership asked for urgent military assistance (over 20 requests in 1979). The Soviets decided on equipment and advisers but no troops.

title: Andropov-Gromyko-Ustinov-Ponomarev Report to CC CPSU on the Situation in Afghanistan, June 28, 1979
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Report to the Central Committee on the situation in Afghanistan. Source: CWIHP Bulletin 8-9, pp. 152-153. Together with Docs 5-6, it shows Soviet thinking on the wider geostrategic implications, the Iranian revolution, perceived U.S. goals, and suspected Amin-American cooperation.

title: Minutes of Conversation of General Secretary Brezhnev with Erich Honecker, October 4, 1979
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Minutes of the Brezhnev-Honecker conversation. They shed light on Soviet geostrategic thinking about Afghanistan, the impact of the Iranian revolution, perceived U.S. goals, and suspected Amin-U.S. special services cooperation.

title: AmEmbassy Kabul cable 7502 to SecState, "President Amin's Desire for Better Relations"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: [Confidential] Amin reached out to the Americans in early October 1979; Amstutz reports "The Afghan president made clear to me that he is open to see any designated USG mission chief." Amstutz advised against a meeting given his imminent departure on leave, a garrison mutiny against Amin, and a deplorable series of executions by the Amin regime.

title: AmEmbassy Kabul cable 7726 to SecState, "Meeting with President Amin"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: Report on Archer Blood's forty minutes alone with Amin on October 27, 1979, a missing link to Soviet paranoia. The Soviet record shows the meeting set off alarm bells for KGB chief Andropov. Blood concluded Amin genuinely wanted better U.S.-Afghan relations but seemed oblivious to how it would look in Moscow. Also published in FRUS 1977-80, Afghanistan, Vol. XII, pp. 218-222.

title: Report on Afghanistan to the Central Committee CPSU, by A. Gromyko, Y. Andropov, D. Ustinov, B. Ponomarev
authors: A. Gromyko, Y. Andropov, D. Ustinov, B. Ponomarev (published in Lyakhovsky)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: Crucial end-of-October 1979 report to the Central Committee from the Politburo subcommittee assessing Afghanistan. It points to the importance of Amin's meeting with the Americans and the suspicions it raised in Moscow, including the need to prevent counter-revolution or Amin's political re-orientation towards the West.

title: Andropov-Gromyko-Ustinov-Ponomarev Report to the CC CPSU on the Situation in Afghanistan, October 29, 1979
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Report on the situation in Afghanistan reflecting Soviet concerns about the regional impact of the Iranian revolution, perceived U.S. goals, and suspected Amin cooperation with American special services, adding to Soviet urgency.

title: Personal Memorandum from Andropov to Brezhnev, early December 1979
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Unusual personal memo that, per Anatoly Dobrynin, was especially influential in changing Brezhnev's position on sending troops into Afghanistan. Source: CWIHP Bulletin 8-9, pp. 159-160.

title: Andropov handwritten memo to Brezhnev, early December 1979
authors: Yuri Andropov (KGB), transcribed by Anatoly Dobrynin from the Kremlin Archive (APRF)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: Known only because Dobrynin transcribed it at the Presidential Archive in 1995. It is the KGB head's direct recommendation to Brezhnev that the Soviets replace Afghan Communist leader Amin because he might go over to the Americans.

title: Soviet Decisions in December 1979
authors: Gen. Alexander Lyakhovsky, The Tragedy and Valor of the Afghani (1995), pp. 109-112
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: English translation of Gen. Lyakhovsky's authoritative section on Soviet decisions on Afghanistan in December 1979, based on near-complete access to Defense Ministry and Central Committee records. It covers Ustinov's agreement with Andropov and the 75,000-troop plan, and cites threats such as U.S. missiles, CIA activity and possible Pakistani annexation.

title: "On the Situation in 'A'"
authors: Konstantin Chernenko (handwritten, for Politburo/CPSU Central Committee)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: Hand-written one-pager scribbled by Chernenko at a small meeting in Brezhnev's office on December 12, 1979 (Andropov, Ustinov, Gromyko, Suslov, Brezhnev). It became the resolution sending Soviet troops to Afghanistan, showing Andropov's leading role and the lack of wider Politburo debate. From Fond 89, released 1992; CWIHP Bulletin Fall 1994.

title: "When and why the decision to send troops was made"
authors: Georgy M. Kornienko (memoir, The Cold War: Testimony of a Participant)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: Excerpt from the memoirs of Georgy Kornienko, top deputy to Foreign Minister Gromyko, giving an insider view of Gromyko's thinking and Soviet decision-making on Afghanistan in 1979, and pointing to October 1979 as the turning point in Gromyko's thinking about Amin.

title: Situation in A. Handwritten CC CPSU Politburo Decision to Introduce Troops into Afghanistan, December 12, 1979
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Handwritten Politburo decision signed by Politburo members, "On the Situation in A". It is the only documentary evidence of the highly secret decision to send Soviet troops into Afghanistan.

title: Memorandum for The President from Zbigniew Brzezinski, "Reflections on Soviet Intervention in Afghanistan"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: Brzezinski's analysis set the stage for the forceful U.S. response, including grain embargoes and ramped-up covert support to the Afghan guerrillas. It lays out the "arc of crisis" and Moscow's "age-long dream" of Indian Ocean access. Redactions at declassification concerned Pakistan, including that Pakistan's security policy cannot be dictated by nonproliferation policy. Brzezinski cautions against being sanguine about a Soviet Vietnam.

note: DIA's analysis of the war indicates it saw the Russians in a very difficult situation: "We believe the Soviets would have to double their strength to break the current stalemate."

authors: KGB USSR and Soviet General Staff
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Report stating that the Soviet Commander of the Turkmen Military District and the Main Soviet Adviser in Afghanistan were ordered to capture an American citizen working with the mujahedeen. Source: Lyakhovsky, Tragedy and Valor of Afghan, p. 263, trans. Savranskaya.

title: Memorandum of Mikhail Gorbachev's Conversation with Babrak Karmal, March 14, 1985
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: In his first conversation with Afghan leader Karmal, installed by Soviet troops in December 1979, Gorbachev stressed that Soviet troops cannot stay in Afghanistan forever and that the revolution was in its national-democratic stage. He urged Karmal to broaden the regime's base to unite all progressive forces and rely on his own forces.

title: The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan: Five Years After
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Review of the Soviet invasion after five years, showing that by May 1985 the CIA estimated Russian and allied losses as greater than those of the rebels, an unusual condition in guerrilla warfare.

title: Senior Interagency Group Meeting on Follow-up to the visit of Indian Prime Minister Gandhi, June 20
authors: Senior Interagency Group (chaired by Under Secretary Armacost)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Summary of conclusions from the SIG meeting after Gandhi's first Washington visit (June 11-15). The U.S. saw a chance for a new stage in relations and to wean India from reliance on the USSR. It welcomed Gandhi's interest in a more active role on Afghanistan and proposed briefing the Indians on U.S.-Soviet talks and Cordovez negotiations.

title: Iranian Support to the Afghan Resistance
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: DIA analyses from 1985 indicate that Iran and the U.S. both followed their separate interests in supporting the Afghan rebel movement, despite U.S. hostility toward Iran; may have implications for current parallel U.S. and Iranian statements on terrorism.

title: Anatoly Chernyaev Diary, October 17, 1985
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: At the Politburo session of Oct 17, 1985, Gorbachev proposed a final decision on Afghanistan, quoted citizens' letters on dissatisfaction with the war, and described telling Karmal 'we will help you, but with arms only, not troops.' Chernyaev noted Gorbachev's negative reaction to Defense Minister Sokolov's assessment.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable, "Subject: Gandhi's visit to Moscow"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Dean reports on Indian officials' accounts of Gandhi's Moscow stopover. Gandhi focused on disarmament and Pakistan's nuclear bomb with Gorbachev, and regretted that the U.S. would not talk about guarantees after a Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan.

title: Memorandum of Conversation: Reagan-Gorbachev, Second Plenary Meeting, Geneva, November 19, 1985
authors: U.S. record of Reagan-Gorbachev summit (Ronald Reagan Presidential Library)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Serious US-Soviet dialogue on Afghanistan started in 1985. At Geneva Gorbachev said the Soviets were ready for a package solution: non-aligned Afghanistan, Soviet troop withdrawal, refugee return and international guarantees. Reagan supported 'mutual withdrawal of all outside forces', working through the UN, and a 'coalition of Islamic states' to supervise elections. A month earlier the Politburo had decided in principle to withdraw.

title: Reagan Letter to Gandhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Reagan writes ahead of Gandhi's meeting with Zia ul-Haq about nuclear competition in the subcontinent. On Afghanistan, he says the U.S. told UN Secretary General Perez de Cuellar it was ready to accept the draft instrument on international guarantees, provided Soviet troop withdrawal is resolved.

title: Information Memorandum from Richard W. Murphy to Mr. Armacost. Subject: Where We Stand in our Relationship with India
authors: Richard W. Murphy, Department of State
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Describes stagnation or deterioration in U.S.-Indian relations after unrealistic expectations following Gandhi's 1985 visit. Blames continued U.S. support for Pakistan and its covert nuclear program. Suggests initiatives such as technology sales and high-level dialogue; Pakistan arms sales listed as a pitfall.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable, "Subject: Congressman Solarz' Meeting with Prime Minister Gandhi, May 28"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Detailed summary of the Solarz-Gandhi meeting. Covers India-Pakistan relations, Gandhi's questioning of U.S. arms sales (Harpoon, tanks, F-16s) to Pakistan, his suspicions about Pakistan's nuclear weapons, and his view that Gorbachev is ahead of the U.S. on arms proposals.

title: Politburo Session, June 26, 1986
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: The Politburo discusses first results of Najibullah's national reconciliation policy. Gorbachev stresses the withdrawal decision is firm, but the US seems a problem; he proposes early partial withdrawals and pulling the USA and Pakistan to participate more actively.

title: Politburo Session, November 13, 1986
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan Déjà vu? Lessons from the Soviet Experience
note: The first detailed Politburo discussion of the process and difficulties of withdrawing Soviet troops from Afghanistan, including the testimony of Marshal Sergei Akhromeev.

title: Reagan Letter to Gandhi on Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: [Secret] Secret letter before Gandhi's meeting with Gorbachev. Reagan urges Gandhi to press for Soviet withdrawal, says the U.S. does not seek to bleed the Soviets, calls the partial withdrawal phony, and justifies stepped-up security support for Pakistan including early warning capability.

title: Ambassador Dean's Cable- "Subject: Meeting with Prime Minister Gandhi, December 6"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Private conversation focused on Gandhi's summit with Gorbachev and concerns about arming the mujahedin. Gandhi praises Gorbachev, criticizes Weinberger's visit and AWACS for Pakistan, and mentions co-mingling of Iran arms sale funds with mujahedin funding.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable, "Subject: Afghanistan"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Dean summarizes Foreign Secretary Venkateswaran's briefing on the Gandhi-Gorbachev discussion of Afghanistan. Soviets seemed willing to withdraw in 1.5-2 years; Indians suspect elements in Pakistan don't want a solution because of U.S. aid. Dean suggests using India's good offices.

title: Politburo Session, January 21, 1987
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan Déjà vu? Lessons from the Soviet Experience
note: The Politburo discusses the results of Shevardnadze and Dobrynin's trip to Afghanistan. Shevardnadze's report is blunt and pessimistic about the war and the internal situation. The Politburo's main concern is how to end the war but save face and ensure a friendly, neutral Afghanistan.

title: Cable from Secretary of State: Letter to President from Prime Minister Gandhi
authors: Secretary of State (transmitting letter from Rajiv Gandhi)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Text of Gandhi's January 7, 1987 letter to Reagan. Gandhi says the USSR wants to withdraw in a realistic time-frame, accuses Pakistan of exploiting Afghanistan to acquire arms such as AWACS, and laments Reykjavik's breakdown.

title: The Costs of Soviet Involvement in Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Major CIA study examining all aspects of Russian involvement in Afghanistan and detailing costs, concluding they had grown steadily and would likely continue to rise but probably would not change Soviet larger purposes.

title: Politburo Session, February 23, 1987
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: Gorbachev discusses withdrawing while engaging the US and Pakistan in negotiations on a final settlement. He is willing to meet Pakistani leader Zia ul Haq, maybe offering a payoff, and worries about Soviet reputation among non-aligned countries and national liberation movements.

title: Politburo Session, February 26, 1987
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: Gorbachev repeatedly returns to the need to withdraw Soviet troops while struggling with how to explain it, not opening discussion on who is to blame. Gromyko admits introducing troops was a mistake but notes it followed 11 requests from the Afghan government.

title: Reagan Letter to Gandhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Reply to Gandhi's January 7 letter. Reagan announces positive decisions on a supercomputer, INSAT 1-D and LCA, expresses skepticism that Soviet national reconciliation is anything but preserving Najibullah, and promises to press Pakistan on its nuclear program.

title: Memorandum of Conversation between Mikhail Gorbachev and Rajiv Gandhi, July 2, 1987
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Gorbachev trusted Rajiv Gandhi as an intermediary on Afghanistan. Gorbachev explains 'national reconciliation' and Gandhi cautions him about dealing with tribal society. Gorbachev complains that UN negotiator Cordovez talks only about troop withdrawal, and alleges the US pressured Pakistan to keep Soviet troops in Afghanistan longer. He calls the US position 'the main obstacle' to a political settlement.

title: Cable from Ambassador Dean to Secretary of State: "Subject: Discussion with Rajiv Gandhi on Afghanistan"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Dean summarizes Gandhi's July 10 account of his meeting with Gorbachev. Gandhi doubts Najibullah's national reconciliation, and found Gorbachev more concerned about fundamentalism than about Western-backed moderates, and not opposed to a role for the former King.

title: Colonel Tsagolov Letter to USSR Minister of Defense Dmitry Yazov on the Situation in Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan Déjà vu? Lessons from the Soviet Experience
note: Criticism of the Soviet policy of national reconciliation in Afghanistan and analysis of the general failures of the Soviet military mission. It is the first open criticism of the Afghan war from within the military establishment. Tsagolov tried to make his criticism public in an interview with Ogonek and was expelled from the Army in 1988.

title: Colonel Tsagolov's Letter to USSR Minister of Defense Dmitry Yazov on the Situation in Afghanistan, August 13, 1987
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Criticism of the policy of national reconciliation and analysis of the failures of the Soviet military mission. It was the first open criticism of the war from within the military; Tsagolov was expelled from the Army in 1988 after an Ogonek interview.

title: Cable from Secretary of State to Amembassy New Delhi: "Subject: Armacost Pre-summit Discussions with Vorontsov on Afghanistan"
authors: Secretary of State to U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Contentious Armacost-Vorontsov discussion before the Reagan-Gorbachev summit on bringing positions closer on Afghanistan and a withdrawal timeframe. Vorontsov accepts Zahir Shah presiding over a loya jirga, criticizes Peshawar leaders, and reads an intelligence report alleging the U.S. ambassador met Hekmatyar, Sayyaf and Rabbani on Oct 21 to undermine national reconciliation.

title: Ambassador Dean's Cable. Subject: Gandhi/Ryzhkov Meeting: Discussion of Afghanistan
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Dean reports a two-hour talk with Rohen Sen on the Gandhi-Ryzhkov discussion of Afghanistan. Soviets and Indians shared a preference for a non-aligned Afghanistan and for keeping fundamentalists from power. Ryzhkov said the Soviets were in touch with all resistance groups and welcomed a larger Indian role.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable. "Subject: Letter from Prime Minister Gandhi for President Reagan"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Gandhi hands Dean a letter for Reagan outlining India's position on Afghanistan, protesting the Senate Appropriations amendment equating Indian and Pakistani nuclear programs, and stating it is in both countries' interest to avoid fundamentalists gaining the upper hand in Afghanistan.

title: Memorandum of Conversation: Reagan-Gorbachev, Working Luncheon, Washington, December 10, 1987
authors: U.S. record of Reagan-Gorbachev summit (Ronald Reagan Presidential Library)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: After the INF Treaty, Gorbachev hoped for a breakthrough on Afghanistan. He says there is no linkage between troop withdrawal and national reconciliation, but there is one to the US halting supplies to the resistance. Shultz says that after signing, troop withdrawal begins and 60 days later American support will cease. Only the withdrawal timetable remained open.

title: Reagan Letter to Gandhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Reagan responds to Gandhi's December 4 letter, reflecting on Afghanistan talks with Gorbachev at the summit. He says Gorbachev is wedded to Najibullah's coalition approach, and notes no movement on Afghanistan despite the INF Treaty.

title: Gandhi Letter to Reagan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Gandhi congratulates Reagan on the INF treaty and informs him of his meeting with Najibullah and Indian outreach to Zahir Shah and other groups inside and outside Afghanistan to facilitate a stable, representative political order.

title: Reagan Message to Rajiv Gandhi circa mid-February 1988
authors: President Reagan (via Ambassador John Gunther Dean)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Reagan thanks Gandhi for advance word of Gorbachev's withdrawal statement and restates the US bottom line: complete, irreversible Soviet withdrawal, Afghan self-determination and refugee return. He dismisses Gandhi's fears of a fundamentalist takeover, claiming the resistance is moderate, and says the Najibullah regime cannot hold power without the Soviet Army.

title: Gandhi Letter to Reagan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Gandhi recalls U.S. welcome of India's active role, says India contacted groups in and outside Afghanistan, and warns of Gorbachev's forthcoming announcement that withdrawal begins May 15 and finishes in ten months.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable, "Subject: Indian Handling of Afghanistan"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Action cable describing Indian leaders' confusion over the U.S. reaction to Indian efforts on an Afghan settlement. Gandhi perceives that Washington resents increased Indian activism; Kaul was given a démarche about a meeting with Zahir Shah in Rome. Dean suggests a reassuring Reagan letter.

title: Secretary of State Cable to Amembassy New Delhi: "Subject: Recent Demarches on Afghanistan and P.K. Kaul's Reaction"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Shultz's stern reply to Dean. U.S. encouraged Indian activism only to foster realism in Moscow, not to shape Afghan political arrangements. Indian outreach to factions and Zahir Shah is unwelcome, and he questions the reporting from New Delhi.

title: Memorandum of Conversation: The Secretary's Third Meeting with Shevardnadze, February 21, 1988
authors: U.S. Department of State (Dennis Ross Collection, Reagan Library)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Shultz and Shevardnadze discuss Afghanistan along with the Iran-Iraq war, the Middle East and Central America. The US demands a pledge to cease Soviet military aid to Kabul once an agreement takes effect. Shevardnadze explains the difficulty of abandoning the Kabul government, doubts US willingness to guarantee the accords, and the two end no closer to agreement.

title: Excerpt from Record of Conversation between Mikhail Gorbachev and George Shultz, February 22, 1988
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: The Afghanistan portion was the most difficult of a long conversation. Shultz welcomes Gorbachev's Feb 8 statement and hopes the next Geneva round will be the last. Gorbachev furiously accuses the US of changing its position on Mujahedin support since the December summit, while still prioritizing US cooperation and signing the Geneva Accords.

title: Cable from Amembassy New Delhi to Secretary of State. "Subject: Letter from Gandhi to President Reagan on Narcotics, Afghanistan"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Text of Gandhi's February 26 letter on the U.S.-Indian narcotics working group and declining heroin production. It notes that disturbed conditions on the Afghan-Pakistan border are a major source of the problem and add to India's stake in an early Afghan settlement.

title: USSR: Withdrawal from Afghanistan (SNIE 11/37/88, Key Judgments only)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Excerpts from a March 1988 SNIE giving an American assessment of a "firm" Soviet decision, based on a "leadership consensus," to withdraw from Afghanistan. Originally published in CIA, At Cold War's End (1999).

title: Memorandum of Conversation: Secretary's First One-on-One with Shevardnadze, March 21, 1988
authors: U.S. Department of State (Dennis Ross Collection, Reagan Library)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Final ministerial before the Geneva Accords signing. Shevardnadze urges Shultz to limit US support for radical resistance forces, noting Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's election as Peshawar alliance leader and calling him 'a fundamentalist, a person of extreme views'. Shultz insists on 'symmetry'. Shevardnadze proposes a 'third option' dropping the arms-supply issue, and talks pass to deputies Adamishin and Armacost.

title: Memorandum of Conversation: Special Working Group on Afghanistan, March 22, 1988
authors: U.S. Department of State (Dennis Ross Collection, Reagan Library)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Armacost and Adamishin seek to limit arms flows under the 'third option'. Armacost insists on symmetry: if the USSR arms Kabul, the US must be able to arm the resistance via Pakistan, and the Soviets must not accuse Pakistan of violations. Adamishin warns this would undercut the Geneva accords; the exchange grows heated.

title: Memorandum of Conversation: Secretary's Fourth Restricted Session with Shevardnadze, March 23, 1988
authors: U.S. Department of State (Dennis Ross Collection, Reagan Library)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Shultz asks Shevardnadze for informal assurances that the Soviets will not criticize Pakistan for violating the Geneva Accords, since Pakistan was the only realistic supply route to the resistance. After a US caucus the US adds a demand for a moratorium on arms shipments, which Shevardnadze rejects, and he later expresses acute disappointment. Both sides move toward mutual restraint.

title: Powell Letter to Shultz, April 15, 1988
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Angry letter the day after the Geneva Accords signing. Powell criticizes Shultz for the word 'restraint' in his unilateral statement ('meet restraint with restraint'), saying the President believes the Mujahedin will be supplied as needed and not by comparison to Soviet supplies to Kabul.

title: Excerpt from Record of Conversation between Mikhail Gorbachev and George Shultz, April 22, 1988
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: A week after the Geneva signing, Gorbachev reaffirms a neutral, non-aligned Afghanistan and warns that Iranian PM Mousavi and an envoy of Zia ul-Haq spoke of deposing the regime and creating a fundamentalist union of Islamic countries. Shultz denies Pakistan wants that. Gorbachev calls Afghanistan a test of US-Soviet cooperation.

title: Afghanistan: Soviet Withdrawal Scenario
authors: Defense Intelligence Agency, Defense Intelligence Appraisal
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: May 1988 DIA report examining plans for Soviet military withdrawal agreed between Russian diplomats and a UN negotiating team representing U.S., Pakistani, Afghan rebel and other interests.

title: CC CPSU Letter on Afghanistan, May 10, 1988
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: Closed internal letter to all Party members on withdrawal of troops from Afghanistan, analyzing events, Soviet actions, problems faced by troops, overlooked historic and ethnic factors, Soviet interests and reasons for withdrawal.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable to Secretary of State. Subject: Meeting with Prime Minister Gandhi, June 3
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: 50-minute conversation in which Gandhi criticizes Zia's dismissal of Junejo, argues U.S. arms to Pakistan lack a basis after Soviet withdrawal, and says India backs Najibullah only to keep extremists like Hekmatyar from power. He asks whether Pakistan's nuclear progress is an Islamic nuclear force and discusses AWACS.

title: Cable from Ambassador Raphel, Islamabad, to Secretary of State, Washington: "Subject: USCINCCENT Visit to Pakistan: The Pak Military on Afghanistan"
authors: Ambassador Arnold Raphel, U.S. Embassy Islamabad
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Conversations of Gen. George Crist and Raphel with Gen. Akhtar Abdul Rahman and Gen. Aslam Beg. Pakistani generals discuss unseating Najib, keeping the mujahedin united, delaying refugee returns, and an Islamic republic in Afghanistan joining Pakistan, Turkey and Iran in a bloc. Raphel concludes the Paks feel a new phase has started in the perennial great game.

title: Cable from Amembassy Islamabad for Under Secretary Armacost and Ambassador Dean from Raphel. "Subject: Indo-Pakistani Relations"
authors: Ambassador Arnold Raphel, U.S. Embassy Islamabad
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Raphel agrees with Dean that Pakistan looks beyond the Soviet withdrawal to a new great game and a grand Islamic coalition from Turkey to Pakistan. For Americans the withdrawal is the victory; for South Asians it is only the first act.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable to Secretary of State. "Subject: Sale of AWACS to Pakistan"
authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Dean criticizes Zia for dismissing his prime minister and national assembly, and urges holding AWACS notification in abeyance until Zia shows commitment to democracy.

title: Ambassador Dean Cable to Secretary of State. Subject: Meeting with Gopi Arora, June 18: Afghanistan
authors: U.S. Embassy New Delhi (Ambassador John Gunther Dean)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Dean reports on Gopi Arora's briefing on his meeting with Dobrynin. Arora believes Gorbachev is committed to full withdrawal, that the PDPA is stronger than the Mujahedin claim, and that India backs Najibullah's aim of keeping extreme fundamentalists out of Kabul. He asks whether US interests parallel Zia's; Dean says the US saw no role for Najibullah.

title: Gandhi Letter to Reagan, August 3, 1988
authors: Rajiv Gandhi, Prime Minister of India
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: As the Soviets finished withdrawing half their troops, the radical resistance was organizing and less willing to negotiate. Gandhi warns Reagan against 'encouragement of fundamentalism', saying a fundamentalist regime in Kabul would not serve India or the US and cannot be reconciled with democracy and human rights.

title: Cable from Ambassador Oakley, Amembassy Islamabad: "Subject: Ambassador Oakley's Meeting with General Beg"
authors: Ambassador Robert Oakley, U.S. Embassy Islamabad
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
note: Oakley meets Army Chief Gen. Mirza Aslam Beg after Zia's death. Beg claims India, the USSR and Afghanistan are destabilizing Pakistan, envisions a strategic consensus of Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, and says the resistance could choke Soviet withdrawal routes; Hekmatyar and Rabbani would not cede power.

title: Minutes of the Session of CC CPSU Politburo, January 23, 1989
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Politburo session on troop withdrawal, the post-war Soviet role in Afghanistan, and possible future developments. Source: CWIHP Bulletin 8-9, pp. 181-184.

title: Politburo Session, January 24, 1989
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: Session on completing the withdrawal and the post-war Soviet role in Afghanistan. It shows a split in the leadership, with Shevardnadze arguing for leaving personnel behind to protect the Najibullah regime or delaying full withdrawal.

title: National Security Directive 3. Subject: U.S. Policy Toward Afghanistan, February 13, 1989
authors: White House (Bush administration, National Security Council)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Issued two days before the last Soviet soldier left, the heavily redacted directive reaffirms Reagan policy of supporting the resistance and 'working in concert with Pakistan'. It shows the US expected Najibullah's imminent fall, rejected Soviet proposals limiting US options on aid, and would treat Soviet bombing after Feb 15 as a Geneva violation.

title: Excerpt from Statement of the Soviet Military Command in Afghanistan on the Withdrawal of Soviet Troops, February 14, 1989
authors: Soviet Military Command in Afghanistan / USSR Defense Ministry
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan and the Soviet Withdrawal 1989 20 Years Later
note: Statement delivered to the head of the UN Mission in Afghanistan on Feb 14, 1989. It reviews Soviet-Afghan relations before 1979, justifies sending troops after repeated Afghan requests, criticizes US arming of the opposition despite the Geneva agreements, and rejects Vietnam comparisons.

title: Excerpt from Statement of the Soviet Military Command in Afghanistan on the Withdrawal of Soviet Troops, February 14, 1989
authors: Soviet Military Command in Afghanistan / USSR Defense Ministry
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Statement delivered to the head of the UN Mission on the day the last Soviet soldier left. It reviews Soviet-Afghan relations, justifies the intervention, criticizes U.S. arming of the opposition in disregard of the Geneva agreements, and rejects Vietnam comparisons. Source: Lyakhovsky, Appendix 11.

title: Lessons from the War in Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Mid-1989 Army report on lessons learned from the Afghan war; heavily excised, but illustrates how much the U.S. ascertained from observing events in Afghanistan.

title: Archer K. Blood Oral History Excerpt
authors: Archer K. Blood, ADST Foreign Affairs Oral History Project (interview by Henry Precht)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
note: Blood describes the situation in Afghanistan and how he came to substitute for Amstutz. He explains, via the Indians, why the Afghans would never approve his return to Kabul as head of mission because of his "secret meetings with Amin." Also recalls his 1971 Dhaka dissent cable.

title: Memorandum of Conversation: Baker-Shevardnadze Ministerial in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Second Small Group Meeting (Regional Issues), September 22, 1989
authors: U.S. Department of State (Bush Presidential Library)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: Yuri Alekseyev presents the Najibullah settlement plan: guiding council, monitored free elections, new constitution and an international conference with the US, USSR, Iran, Pakistan and China. Condoleezza Rice says the resistance would not accept the present government's composition; Baker says Najibullah's name should be taken off for the plan to fly.

title: Afghanistan: The War in Perspective (SNIE 37-89, Key Judgments only)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: November 1989 SNIE reckons that despite military withdrawal the Soviets will provide "massive aid" to their client regime, while Kabul will try to negotiate separate truces with "local resistance commanders." Originally published in CIA, At Cold War's End (1999).

title: Excerpt from Record of Conversation between Mikhail Gorbachev and James Baker, February 9, 1990
authors: Gorbachev Foundation / Bush Presidential Library record
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: In Moscow, Baker and Gorbachev discuss an Afghan political settlement. Both prefer a political solution and independent Afghanistan but admit limited influence over Afghan parties. Gorbachev promotes the Najibullah plan of UN-monitored elections; Baker says the Mujahedin cannot be persuaded. Both say 'let them boil in their own juices'.

title: Memorandum of Conversation between Secretary Baker and Eduard Shevardnadze, March 20, 1990
authors: U.S. Department of State (Mandatory Review M-2017-16468)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
note: In Namibia, Baker and Shevardnadze seek a solution on Afghanistan. The US demands Najibullah go and not stand in elections; Shevardnadze argues for UN-monitored free elections. He says no Mujahedin leader will accept free elections: 'They all have a dictatorial persuasion—Hekmatiyar, Khalis—you name it.'

title: Funding of the Gama'at al-Islamiya by Wealthy Saudi Oppositionist Usama Bin Ladin; Composition of Sudanese Wing of the Egyptian Gama'at al-Islamiya
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on bin Ladin's funding of the Egyptian Gama'at al-Islamiya and the composition of its Sudanese wing. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 1.

title: Georgy Kornienko's Account of the Politburo Decision to Send Soviet Troops in Afghanistan, from The Cold War: Testimony of a Participant (Moscow, 1994), pp. 193-195
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Memoir excerpt by the former Deputy Foreign Minister giving a detailed account of how the final decision to send troops was made.

title: New Fighting and New Forces in Kandahar
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Consular officials report on a stranded Pakistani aid convoy and fighting between Afghan factions in Kandahar. One party is a new movement, the Taliban ("Seekers"), which had taken Spin Boldak and came from madrasas in Quetta and Peshawar. Speculation about who supports Mullah Omar's Taliban is rife. The movement may be a new phenomenon independent of party politics. Excised.

title: Weekly South Asia Activity Report
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Weekly report on South Asia developments: Afghan refugees fleeing Kabul, the UN Mestiri mission, and the stranded Pakistani convoy. It mentions the debriefing of British kidnapping victims who identified their captor as "Rohit Sharma", i.e. Ahmed Omar Saeed Sheikh, later the self-confessed mastermind of the Daniel Pearl kidnapping.

title: The Taliban - Who Knows What the Movement Means?
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Discusses the suspected origins, goals and sponsors of the Taliban, which now controls most of Kandahar province. The Rabbani/Masoud government is worried by the Taliban's rapid growth. The Taliban offer hope to war-weary Afghans disgusted with national leaders' failure to compromise.

title: Developments in Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Unknown] As the Taliban emerge as a major player, a source (name excised) is troubled by Pakistan's deep involvement in Afghan politics and its role in the Taliban's recent successes. He says the ISI is deeply involved in the Taliban takeover of Kandahar and Qalat, and that Pakistan's agenda will sabotage UN peace efforts led by Mahmoud Mestiri.

title: Developments in Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Unknown] Memo to the State Department Afghanistan Desk showing concern over ISI involvement in the Taliban takeover of Kandahar. A handwritten note says "This AM I've heard that General Babar is running this Taliban op." Babar was the Pashtun Pakistani Interior Minister.

title: [Excised] Believe Pakistan is Backing Taliban
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Secret] Conveys a source's belief that Pakistan directly supports the Taliban, with General Babar as principal patron. Pakistani Frontier Corps allegedly provided artillery cover for the Taliban's seizure of the Spin Boldak arms dump.

title: UN document on the Kabul mob attack on the Pakistani embassy after the Taliban takeover of Herat (title not given on page)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: Linked from the Document 4 summary. UN officials independently agree with Ambassador Humayun that the loss of Herat to the Taliban could not have provoked any spontaneous outbursts, implying the Kabul mob attack on Pakistan's embassy was organized.

title: Alexander Lyakhovsky's Account of the Decision of the CC CPSU to Send Troops to Afghanistan
authors: Alexander Lyakhovsky, The Tragedy and Valor of Afghan (Moscow, 1995)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), SOVIET INVASION OF AFGHANISTAN A CASE OF MISSION CREEP, ACCORDING TO NEW BOOK AND ORIGINAL SOVIET DOCUMENTS
url: https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB396/docs/Lyakhovsky, Decision to send troops into Afghanistan.pdf
note: Lyakhovsky's account of the CC CPSU decision to send troops to Afghanistan, from The Tragedy and Valor of Afghan (Moscow, 1995).

title: Alexander Lyakhovsky's Account of the Decision of the CC CPSU to Send Troops to Afghanistan, from The Tragedy and Valor of Afghan (Moscow, 1995)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Memoir/book excerpt giving a detailed account of how the final decision to send troops was made. The only documentary evidence of that secret decision is the handwritten Dec. 12, 1979 document.

title: On the Changing Mission of the Soviet Forces in Afghanistan, from Alexander Lyakhovsky, The Tragedy and Valor of Afghan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
note: Excerpt describing how the first combat operations changed the Limited Contingent's original mission to include combat against the rebels.

title: The Taliban: What We've Heard
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Secret] Relays observations of recent visitors to Kandahar. The Taliban are well armed, militarily proficient and eager to expand to end banditry and impose Sharia. Women are ordered to stay home and male doctors are barred from treating female patients.

title: Northern Afghan Strongman General Dostam Meets Taliban Representatives (Islama 00975)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Pakistani officials allegedly tell Gen. Dostum not to worry about the Taliban because Pakistan can take care of them, and he reportedly agrees to cooperate with the Taliban on opening trade routes. Taliban officials tell him they have no territorial ambitions in the north. The Taliban would seize Mazar-e-Sharif in May 1997.

title: Meeting with the Taliban in Kandahar: More Questions than Answers
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Reports on the Taliban's plans to take Kabul, disarm rival commanders and install one government. Shows the beginnings of Taliban double-talk, wanting peace but saying "anyone who gets in our way will be crushed." Financial support and drug policy are also discussed.

title: Eyewitness to the Fall of Herat Says Taliban are Winning Hearts and Minds - For Now
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] An American citizen who witnessed the fall of Herat faults Ismail Khan's political and military ineptitude. He says the Taliban were extremely well organized, well-financed and strongly disciplined.

title: Finally, A Talkative Talib: Origins and Membership of the Religious Students' Movement
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Based on a Talib source, offers an in-depth sketch of Mullah Mohammed Omar and the creation and organization of the Taliban. The source denies foreign patronage and says the movement disliked Saudi interference and ISI efforts to treat Afghanistan like another province. Also raises the expiring Durand Accord and Pashtunistan.

title: Rabbani Emissary States Rabbani Will Not Surrender Power to Interim Council Until Taliban Join
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Embassy officials meet Rabbani's Economic Advisor Ashraf Shah, who summarizes events including Taliban capture of Charasiab, Maydan Shahr, Chowk-i-Wardak and the Ghazni-Kabul road. He says the government would probably not give up power to an Interim Council until the Taliban agreed to join.

title: The Harakat-ul-Ansar - The Pakistan Dimension [Excised] (Karachi 01617)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Haqqani History: Bin Ladin's Advocate Inside the Taliban
note: [Secret] Report on the Kashmiri militant group Harakat-ul-Ansar. Many of its activists are Afghan war veterans who fought with Maulana Jalaluddin Haqqani in Paktia. A significant portion of the membership is non-Pakistani, including veterans from Algeria, Tunisia, Sudan, Egypt and elsewhere. Three sources say the membership also includes a small number of American Muslims, with estimates ranging from six to sixteen.

title: The Harakat-ul-Ansar - The Pakistan Dimension [Excised] (Karachi 01617)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Haqqani History: Bin Ladin's Advocate Inside the Taliban
note: [Secret] Report on the Kashmiri militant group Harakat-ul-Ansar. Many of its activists are Afghan war veterans who fought with Maulana Jalaluddin Haqqani in Paktia. A significant portion of the membership is non-Pakistani, including veterans from Algeria, Tunisia, Sudan, Egypt and elsewhere. Three sources say the membership also includes a small number of American Muslims, with estimates ranging from six to sixteen.

title: PDD 39, U.S. Policy on Counterterrorism
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
note: [Secret] 12-page directive on reducing vulnerabilities, deterring and responding to terrorism, and WMD. It directs the FBI, Transportation, the DCI (aggressive intelligence collection, analysis, counterintelligence and covert action) and FEMA. It states the U.S. will induce cooperation from states harboring wanted terrorists and may return suspects by force without host government cooperation.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Take Shindand Air Base; Herat Threatened - Will Iran Intervene
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Reports the Taliban seizure of Shindand Air Base, previously held by Ismail Khan, and their advance on Herat. Discusses possible Iranian reactions to the Taliban threat.

title: Afghanistan: Heavy Fighting Rages West of Kabul; Herat Calm After Taliban Take-Over
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] The Taliban take Herat, forcing Ismail Khan and 300-600 followers into Iran. Hekmatyar's forces are attacked by Masoud's government troops. A crowd set fire to the Pakistani Embassy in Kabul in response to Pakistan's support for the Taliban.

title: A/S Raphel's October 4 Meeting with Assef Ali on Afghanistan (State 243042)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Pakistan Foreign Minister Assef Ali tells Assistant Secretary Robin Raphel that Pakistan's message to the Rabbani opposition was to unite against Kabul but not attack it. He does not deny significant Pakistani contact with and some support for the Taliban, saying little outside material support was needed given their Pashtun support.

title: Pakistan Afghan Policy: Anyone but Rabbani/Massoud - Even the Taliban (Islama 09675)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Pakistan's Ambassador to Afghanistan Qazi Humayun says Pakistan finds itself in the uncomfortable position of backing the Taliban. Relations with the Rabbani government had worsened after a mob destroyed Pakistan's embassy in Kabul in September. Humayun says a Taliban government would in many ways be worse than the present one.

title: Letter of GOP Permrep to SYG on Afghanistan (USUN N 004283)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Unclassified] Reproduces an October 25, 1995 letter from Pakistan's UN representative to the UN Secretary General. It reaffirms Pakistan's claimed neutral stance in intra-Afghan rivalries and its support for UN and OIC peace efforts, illustrating Pakistan's public position.

title: Afghanistan: Russian Embassy Official Claims Iran Interfering more than Pakistan (Islama 11049)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] A Russian Embassy official says Pakistan gives the Taliban modest financial assistance, logistics, fuel and military training and ignores a booming smuggling trade. He says Taliban funding mostly comes from Afghan traders and that Pakistani aid is smaller than Iranian aid to the Rabbani government.

title: Sketch of a South Asia-Based Terrorist Training and Logistic Network, DI TR 95-12
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Analytic Report on a South Asia-based terrorist training and logistics network. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 67.

title: Discussing Afghan Policy with the Pakistanis (State 291940)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] State questions Pakistan's policy of backing any group opposed to the Rabbani government, including the Taliban. It doubts Pakistan can control the Taliban ('falls short of being able to call the shots') and notes Tehran, Moscow and New Delhi wrongly assume the U.S. shares Pakistan's support for the Taliban.

title: Transcription of CIA 1996 biographic sketch, 'Usama Bin Laden: Islamic Extremist Financier'
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Osama Bin Laden File
note: Typed transcription of the CIA's 1996 bio sketch of bin Laden as a financier of Islamic extremist activities.

title: Usama bin Ladin: Islamic Extremist Financier
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
note: [Unclassified] CIA assessment released to the media in 1996. It gives background on bin Ladin, including his role in supporting the resistance to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. It covers his terrorist activities, the Islamic Salvation Foundation (Al-Qaida) and collaboration with other extremist groups. It also traces his commercial activities since 1989 (e.g., construction of an airport near Port Sudan) and reports that by January 1994 he was helping finance three terrorist training camps in northern Sudan.

title: Pakistan-Afghanistan Relations
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] State Department summary of Afghanistan-Pakistan relations and the impact each state has on the other's stability. Covers arms and narco-trafficking effects (lawlessness, arms culture, bombings and assassinations in NWFP), foreign interference from India, Iran, Pakistan and Russia, and U.S. views and policy interests. Says Pakistan lacks a well-conceived end-game for supporting the Taliban and opposing Rabbani.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Official Says Divisions Within Movement Growing; Predicts 'Fight with Iran' (Islama 01403)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] A Taliban official says Pakistan gave ammunition only at the start in 1994 and that the Taliban now capture their own supplies. He adds that Pakistan used Afghan traders to channel money to the Taliban, avoiding a direct link, implying the traders may be conduits for Pakistani government funding.

title: Pak Foreign Minister Asks U.S. Cooperation on Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Acting Secretary Strobe Talbott tells Pakistani Foreign Minister Assef Ali that Pakistani support for the Taliban is forcing Moscow and Tehran to keep aiding Rabbani and Masoud. He draws an analogy between support for the Taliban and for Kashmiri militants, warning of unintended consequences.

title: Senator Brown and Congressman Wilson Discuss Afghanistan with Pakistani Officials
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto meets Senator Hank Brown and Congressman Charlie Wilson. She stresses the need for the Trans-Afghan gas pipeline and says the perception that her government backed the Taliban was simply untrue.

title: A/S Raphel Discusses Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Assistant Secretary Robin Raphel meets Pakistani, Kabul government and Taliban officials. Gen. Karamat calls the Taliban "a millstone around our necks" and Bhutto claims only non-lethal aid. Masoud says Pakistan is as much to blame as the Soviets. The Taliban say "If the U.N. fails, then we have failed."

title: A/S Raphel Consultations with Deputy FM Chernyshev
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Raphel meets Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Chernyshev, mostly about Afghanistan. She notes US interest in peace facilitating the Unocal gas pipeline and proposes an arms embargo. The Russians support the Mestiri mission and deny arming any faction.

title: Harakat ul-Ansar: Increasing Threat to Western and Pakistani Interests (DI TR 96-008)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Secret] Pakistan's ISID provides at least $30,000 and possibly $60,000 per month to Harakat ul-Ansar, though Pakistan may be trimming support to avoid state-sponsor listing. HUA is reaching out to bin Laden and Qadhafi and shifting toward Western targets; contacts hinted at attacks on civilian airliners.

title: Dealing with the Taliban in Kabul
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] After the Taliban takeover of Kabul, State instructs the Embassy in Pakistan to engage the new Taliban interim government on stability, human rights, narcotics and terrorism. Talking points show the desire to locate Osama Bin Laden.

title: National Intelligence Daily (NID 96-0229CX)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Top Secret] Four days after the Taliban took Kabul, the CIA notes the Taliban closed camps tied to Hekmatyar, Sayyaf and Jamaat-i-Islami but not those associated with bin Laden, Hizb-i-Islami (Khalis), Jamiat-Ulema-i-Islam and Harakat ul-Ansar, including HUA's main camp in Khowst.

title: Afghan-Pak Border Relations at Torkham Tense (Peshaw 00916)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] A consulate contact witnessed 30-35 sealed ISI trucks and 15-20 fuel tankers waiting to cross at Torkham and was certain of the convoy's ISI affiliation. The cable does not specify the contents or destination.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Biodata (State 206975)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Thumbnail sketches of Taliban officials, summarizing the emerging leadership weeks after the takeover of Kabul. Gives background on Mullah Omar, Rabbani, Ghaus, Hassan, Ehsanullah, Abbas, Wakil Ahmad and Yar Mohammad. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Seeks Low Profile Relations With the USG – At Least For Now (Islama 08520)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Secret] Abdul Jalil, self-described number two for the Taliban on foreign affairs, delivers a friendly message from Mullah Omar. The Taliban want good relations with the U.S. but unpublicized contacts, to avoid accusations of being an anti-Shia tool of the U.S. Jalil is said to make a good impression and to work for Mullah Ghaus.

title: Central Asian Reaction to Taliban's Takeover of Kabul (Mori Document 1161400)
authors: CIA, Office of Russian and Eurasian Analysis
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Secret] Assessment two weeks after the Taliban takeover of Kabul of Central Asian reaction. Only Pakistan recognizes the Taliban; neighbors are alarmed and fear instability, but have not decided on collective efforts to arm Taliban opponents. Identifies key Taliban figures including Mullah Omar. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Foreign Secretary Mulls over Afghanistan (Islama 08637)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Pakistan Foreign Secretary Najamuddin Shaikh insists Pakistani aid to the Taliban is not increasing and that Pakistan urges the Taliban to cooperate with other factions. Ambassador Simons says the U.S. will keep urging Pakistan not to side with the Taliban.

title: IAC Intelligence Assessment IA 7/96 - Afghanistan: Taliban's Challenges, Regional Concerns
authors: Privy Council Office (Ottawa, Canada), released by U.S. National Security Agency
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Top Secret - SI, Umbra] Canadian assessment a month after the Taliban takeover of Kabul. It sees a country divided between Pakistan-supported Pushtun/Taliban forces and the Tajik/Uzbek/Shia forces of Dostam, Masood and Khalili. Regional neighbors fear the Taliban, and even Pakistan must harbour concern about Taliban links to its own Pashtuns. Kashmiri militants will likely be encouraged.

title: [Excised]/Pakistan Interservice Intelligence/Pakistan Directorate Supplying the Taliban Forces
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Secret] The ISI is supplying the Taliban with munitions, fuel and food, using a private sector transportation company to funnel supplies into Afghanistan. Food convoys are open, but munitions convoys depart late in the evening and are concealed.

title: IIR [Excised] Pakistan Involvement in Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] ISI is heavily involved in Afghanistan. Pakistan's Pashtun-based Frontier Corps is used for command and control, training and combat in Taliban operations, while the Punjabi-dominated regular army is not. Frontier Corps provide training in Kandahar or Herat to Pakistani madrassa students fighting for the Taliban.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Deny They Are Sheltering HUA Militants, Usama bin Laden (Islama 09517)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Ambassador Simons presses Taliban acting foreign minister Mullah Ghaus on HUA militants in Khost camps and bin Laden near Jalalabad. Ghaus denies any foreigners are in Khost and suggests bin Laden left with Hekmatyar. The page adds 9/11 Commission context on bin Laden's return and Pakistani intelligence facilitation.

title: Ambassador Meets Taliban: We are the People
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Ambassador Thomas Simons meets Taliban Acting Foreign Minister Mullah Ghaus on 11 November. Ghaus blames Russia, Iran and India for the ongoing war. Simons says Americans are "the most religious people in the western world." Both agree a negotiated settlement is best, but communication difficulties are evident.

title: Afghanistan: British Journalist Visits Site of Training Camps; HUA Activity Alleged (Islama 009994)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] A British journalist who visited two training camps in Paktia on November 14, 1996 reports both appear occupied. Taliban sources say one is occupied by Harakat-ul-Ansar and the other by assorted foreigners including Chechens, Bosnian Muslims, Sudanese and other Arabs.

title: Terrorism: Historical Background of the Islamic Army, And Bin Ladin's Move from Afghanistan to Sudan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Historical background of the Islamic Army and bin Ladin's move from Afghanistan to Sudan. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnotes 25, 31, 35, 36; Chapter 4, Endnote 3.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Rep Won't Seek UN Seat For Now
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] US officials meet a Taliban representative who says the Taliban want US influence rather than Iranian, Pakistani or Russian. The source describes three internal Taliban factions and extensive Pakistani/ISI support: cash, supplies, military/intelligence advisers and even drafting letters.

title: [Excised] Africa Division Recommendations Regarding Sudan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Memorandum for the Acting Director of Central Intelligence, author excised, giving Africa Division recommendations regarding Sudan. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 7.

title: [Title Excised] The Following Was the Structure of Usama Bin Ladin's Islamic Army
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on the structure of bin Ladin's Islamic Army. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 3.

title: Terrorism: Responsibilities and Background of Islamic Army Shura Council Members
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Responsibilities and background of Islamic Army Shura Council members. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 37.

title: Terrorism: Activities and Functions of the Islamic Army's Military Committee, and Political and Sharia Committee; Process of Approving Terrorist Operations
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on the activities of the Islamic Army's Military Committee and Political and Sharia Committee, and how terrorist operations are approved. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 3.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Shift Yar Mohammad from Herat to Ghazni (Islama 00025)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Mullah Omar moves Mullah Yar Mohammed from the governorship of Herat to Ghazni. The cable questions Omar's motives, including suppressing Yar Mohammad's independent power base, and whether he would accept the move. Excised.

title: Terrorism: Usama Bin Ladin Trying to Develop WMD Capability, CTC 97-30002
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Counterterrorist Center Commentary on bin Ladin trying to develop a WMD capability. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 49.

title: Afghanistan: Jalaluddin Haqqani's Emergence As a Key Taliban Commander (Islama 00154)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Haqqani is reported to be more liberal on social policy than other Taliban but lacks political clout, and is respected as a military commander. His ties to radical Arab groups concern State, as he reportedly offers shelter to Arabs in Paktia in exchange for weapons and money. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Jalaluddin Haqqani's Emergence As a Key Taliban Commander (Islamabad 00154)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Haqqani History: Bin Ladin's Advocate Inside the Taliban
note: [Confidential] Haqqani is reported to be more liberal on social policy such as women's rights than other Taliban officials, but unable to influence Taliban positions. He remains a respected, competent and influential officer in Taliban military affairs. His ties to various radical Arab groups concern the Department of State; one source says that in exchange for weapons and money he offers shelter to Arabs in Paktia province.

title: Terrorism: Fatwa Issued in 1992 by Usama bin Ladin's Islamic Army to Attack U.S. Military in Saudi Arabia, Movement of Explosives [Excised] by the Islamic Army [Excised] to Saudi Arabia [Excised]
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on a 1992 fatwa by the Islamic Army to attack the U.S. military in Saudi Arabia, and on the movement of explosives. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 47.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Agree to Visits of Militant Training Camps, Admit Bin Ladin is Their Guest (1997 Peshaw 00021)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Secret] Taliban Foreign Minister Ghaus and Mullah Rabbani tell U.S. officials to choose a delegation and dates to visit camps the Taliban claim to have closed. Deputy FM Jalil says bin Laden had lived in caves near Tora Bora and was told to move to an ordinary house.

title: [Title Excised] A Fatwa Issued by Usama Bin Ladin's Islamic Army Which Allowed for Attacks Against the U.S. Military in Saudi Arabia
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on a fatwa issued by the Islamic Army allowing attacks on the U.S. military in Saudi Arabia. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 47.

title: Scenesetter for Your Visit to Islamabad: Afghan Angle (Islama 00436)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Background for Robin Raphel's visit. A Taliban government in Kabul would be 'as good as it can get' for Pakistan. The Taliban let HUA use Khost camps, Pakistani aid is 'more significant and probably less malign than most imagine', and Islamabad plays an overbearing role in Taliban political and diplomatic initiatives.

title: Scenesetter for Your Visit to Islamabad: Afghan Angle
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Ambassador Simons briefs Assistant Secretary Raphel before her visit. The Taliban are revered in Kandahar but seen as occupiers in Herat and Kabul. Pakistani aid pushes Iran, and probably Russia and India, to back Masoud and Rabbani. US interests include peace, counterterrorism (expel Bin Ladin), narcotics, humanitarian issues and pipelines.

title: [Title Excised] Usama Bin Ladin's Islamic Army Issued a Series of Fatwas, Most of the Against the United States
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on a series of fatwas issued by the Islamic Army, most against the United States. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 3.

title: Terrorism: Cooperation Among Usama Bin Ladin's Islamic Army, Iran and the NIF
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on cooperation among bin Ladin's Islamic Army, Iran and Sudan's NIF. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 85.

title: Terrorism: Establishment of a Tripartite Agreement Among Usama Bin Ladin, Iran, and the NIF
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on a tripartite agreement among bin Ladin, Iran and the NIF. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 52.

title: Pakistan Counterterrorism: Ambassador's Meeting with [Excised] on State Sponsor Designation (Islama 001054)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Secret] The Embassy raises the HUA-bin Laden-Taliban triangle with a Pakistani official. Both bin Laden and HUA have sanctuary in Afghanistan and Khost camps, and the U.S. fears a link-up with serious consequences. The official says HUA is under enough control and Pakistan will not allow bin Laden to use its territory.

title: Terrorism: Possible Islamic Army Foreknowledge of an Egyptian Operation and Logistical and Security Assistance Provided for the Attackers
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on possible Islamic Army foreknowledge of an Egyptian operation and on logistical and security assistance given to the attackers. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 56.

title: Pakistan [Excised] On Afghanistan, HUA, Bin Laden
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] Reports former Ambassador Robert Oakley's non-official visit to Pakistan and his review of Afghanistan, including long-term dangers of Taliban success. Interlocutors discuss a possible Pushtoon nationalist/Islamic radical blowback, Harkat ul-Ansar (HUA) camps and fighters in Afghanistan with Taliban and UBL approval, and Pakistani leverage over the Taliban. ISI has advocated recognizing the Taliban and warded off Foreign Ministry attempts to close madrassas in the tribal agencies and near the border.

title: Afghanistan: Raising Bin Ladin With the Taliban (Islama 01750)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Confidential] Mullah Ehsanullah Ehsan, an influential member of the Taliban Inner Shura, tells embassy officials that expelling bin Laden is not a solution ('To where and how should he be expelled?'). He says the Taliban did not know where bin Laden was and would ban his activities if he were found in their areas. He argues the real problem is U.S. non-recognition of the Taliban, and claims bin Laden was invited by the Taliban's enemies and gives them no financial help.

title: Terrorism: Usama Bin Ladin's Links to a Southern Yemeni Group
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on bin Ladin's links to a southern Yemeni group. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 44.

title: Official Informal for SA Assistant Secretary Robin Raphel and SA/PAB (Islama 01873)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Fighting will continue as Iran and Russia supply Massoud, while Pakistan appears to review its policy but agencies like ISID remain committed to a Taliban victory. The Taliban continue to protect bin Laden and appear to have a deal, perhaps ISID-brokered, letting HUA use Khost camps. The Embassy recommends limited engagement.

title: Official Informal for SA Assistant Secretary Robin Raphel and SA/PAB (Islama 01873)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] State notes differences of opinion among high-level Taliban leaders and no well-defined process for communicating decisions.
