The Taliban are ideologically heterogeneous, including non-ideological Afghans who joined for their own motives. Concedes the Taliban are a fact of life. Previously published in the August 2007 briefing book on Pakistan. Excised.

title: Afghanistan and Sectarian Violence Contribute to a Souring of Pakistan's Relations with Iran (Islama 02001)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Discusses how Pakistan's Taliban support harms ties with Iran. The U.S. should steer clear of Pakistan-Iran disputes. Pakistan denies being the Taliban's godfather, though officials privately acknowledge close links and supplying foodstuffs and fuel.

title: Terrorism: Usama Bin Ladin's Attempts to Acquire Uranium
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on bin Ladin's attempts to acquire uranium. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 49; Chapter 4, Endnote 3.

title: Terrorism: Usama bin Ladin's Historical Links to Abdullah Azzam
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on bin Ladin's historical links to Abdullah Azzam. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnotes 22, 43.

title: Terrorism: Usama Bin Ladin's Activities in Somalia and Sudanese NIF Support
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on bin Ladin's activities in Somalia and Sudanese NIF support. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 45; Chapter 4, Endnote 3.

title: Afghanistan: GOP denies Pakistani Involvement in Fighting; Taliban Reportedly Enlisting Supporters in Frontier Areas
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] A US officer talks with Pakistani Afghan desk officer Naeem Khan and Taliban Embassy First Secretary Abdul Wahab. Khan denies military aid, admitting only diplomatic support. Wahab denies official Pakistani support but admits manpower from Pakistan's NWFP tribal areas.

title: Terrorism: Usama Bin Ladin's Financial Support to the Egyptian Al-Gama'at Al-Islamiyya, as well as Algerian and Libyan Extremists
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on bin Ladin's financial support to the Egyptian Gama'at al-Islamiyya and to Algerian and Libyan extremists. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 1.

title: Afghanistan: Observers Report Uptick in Support for Anti-Taliban Factions by Iran
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Relays information about Iranian military and political support for anti-Taliban factions. A State source sees it as a strategic reaction to Taliban efforts to control the north, while Pakistanis see it as aggressive.

title: Terrorism: Activities of Bin Ladin's in Pakistan, Afghanistan, and India
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on bin Ladin's activities in Pakistan, Afghanistan and India. The Islamic Army treated Pakistan/Afghanistan as one region, a base and training center supporting insurgencies in Tajikistan, Kashmir and Chechnya, with a camp in Pakistan recruiting mostly Pakistanis. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 67.

title: [Title Excised] Plan to establish an Iraqi Element in Bin Ladin's Islamic Army
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA Intelligence Report on a plan to establish an Iraqi element in bin Ladin's Islamic Army. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 54.

title: Afghanistan: Straight Talk with [Excised]
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] Ambassador Thomas Simons meets a source who appears to be Shamshad Ahmad, Pakistani envoy to the UN, to discuss Pakistani policy toward the Taliban. Ahmad is pleased at the replacement of UNSMA head Norbert Holl and says Pakistan wants to promote inter-Afghan dialogue. Simons warns that any appearance of preference for replacement Lakdar Brahimi will fuel rumors that Pakistan is pro-Taliban.

title: Afghanistan: Pakistanis to Regulate Wheat and Fuel Trade to Gain Leverage Over Taliban (Islama 06882)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Pakistan tightens regulation of wheat and fuel trade with Afghanistan, partly to gain leverage over the Taliban and to curb drug trafficking, demanding hard currency instead of drug 'powder'. Officials say they deal only with the Taliban, and Pakistan continues to back a Taliban takeover.

title: DCI Talking Points Regarding Operations Against Usama Bin Ladin
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: DCI talking points on operations against bin Ladin. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 8.

title: Afghanistan: [Excised] Briefs Ambassador on his Activities. Pleads for Greater Activism by U.N. (Islama 007343)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Previously released in The Taliban File Part III. An excised source describes efforts toward multi-ethnic negotiations. Ambassador Simons says Pakistan has a 'privileged association' with the Taliban but not control, is a party rather than a mediator, and cites 'trucks and busses full of adolescent mujahid' crossing the frontier.

title: Afghanistan: [Excised] Briefs the Ambassador on his Activities. Pleads for Greater Activism by U.N.
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] Unidentified source describes activities supporting a peaceful resolution, including meetings in Tehran, in Dubai with Yunus Qanuni, and in Kandahar with Taliban ministers Mullah Hassan and Mullah Jalil. Ambassador Simons comments that Pakistan's claimed 20 million rupee aid to the Taliban through 1996 excluded Pak wheat and POL and the trucks and buses full of adolescent mujahid with a day or two of weapons training: 'Pakistan's real aid.'

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Official Says that Relations with Russia and Iran "Tense"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Mullah Abdul Jalil tells a US political officer that relations with Russia and Iran are tense. He says the Taliban do not know where Osama Bin Laden or other "Arabs" flushed from training camps are, but are seeking Commander Masoud.

title: Present Pakistani Initiatives in Afghanistan
authors: United Nations Special Mission to Afghanistan (Islamabad)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Unclassified] Norbert Holl reports on his meeting with Pakistan Foreign Ministry official Iftikhar Murshed, who describes Nawaz Sharif's call and meeting with Taliban official Mullah Rabbani, in which Sharif bluntly demanded a goodwill gesture toward other factions and a meeting with President Rabbani. Murshed also comments on the G8 meeting on Afghanistan, the Afghan UN seat and oil embargoes, calling the meeting a non-event.

title: Afghanistan: Meeting with the Taliban
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Taliban officials in the US under Unocal auspices meet Assistant Secretary Karl Inderfurth on 8 December 1997. They seek better relations and crop substitution aid, defend gender policies, and pledge to prevent terrorist use of Afghanistan. They say they did not invite Bin Laden, stopped his public interviews, and frustrated Iranian and Iraqi contact attempts.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Decision-Making and Leadership Structure (Islama 11233)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Secret] Rare insight into Taliban governance as of December 1997: the movement accepted the increasingly personalized rule of Mullah Omar. Describes four structures: the Inner Shura (23 leaders), Outer Shura (100+ members), Caretaker Council under Rabbani, and the Kandahar-based Ulema Shura. Excised.

title: Text of World Islamic Front's Statement Urging Jihad Against Jews and Crusaders
authors: Al Quds al Arabi, via Foreign Broadcast Information Service (Open Source Center)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: [Unclassified] FBIS text of the World Islamic Front statement urging jihad against Jews and Crusaders, published in Al Quds al Arabi. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 1.

title: Afghanistan: [Excised] Describes Pakistan's Current Thinking
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] DCM Alan Eastham meets a source who appears to be Iftikhar Murshed. They review concerns about bin Laden's fatwa, the six plus two process, a proposed Ulema meeting of Taliban and future Northern Alliance, border security, and outside players. Murshed says Pakistan had not provided arms and ammunition to the Taliban for three or four months, apparently the first Pakistani admission of arms supplies.

title: Afghanistan: A Report of Pakistani Military Assistance to the Taliban
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Relays an unconfirmed incident of alleged Pakistani military assistance: 25 large Mercedes Benz trucks full of Pakistani fighters delivered to Kabul airport for transport to Kunduz to assist the Taliban.

title: Afghanistan: The Taliban's Mullah Rabbani: Contender for Taliban Leadership? (Islama 02685)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Rumors of division between Omar and Deputy Leader Rabbani as Rabbani raises his public profile. State does not expect imminent change given the emphasis on unity. Sources conflict on whether Rabbani is a moderate or backs Omar on gender issues and safe haven for bin Laden. Ghaus and Hassan reportedly losing influence. Excised.

title: [Title Excised] "Planning for the UBL Rendition is Going Very Well"
authors: CIA (email to Michael F. Scheuer, from [Excised])
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA email to Michael F. Scheuer, cited in the 9/11 Commission Report as "Capture Op," "[Gary] Schroen to Mike." Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 22.

title: TERRORISM: Bin Ladin Threatening to Attack US Aircraft
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Senior Executive Intelligence Brief, undated, cited in the 9/11 Commission Report as June 1998 (p. 342). Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 11, Endnote 5.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Said to Loosen Grip on Bin Ladin as They Increasingly Turn to Him for Financial Support and Advice (Islamabad 04450)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Haqqani History: Bin Ladin's Advocate Inside the Taliban
note: [Confidential] Sources say Jalaluddin Haqqani is an important advocate for Osama bin Laden within the Taliban administration. Bin Laden appears to operate largely free of Taliban control and to be protected by Taliban elements. His growing autonomy is attributed to the strength of supporters such as Haqqani, who are ideologically close to him and have argued for reducing controls on him.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Said to Loosen Grip on Bin Ladin as They Increasingly Turn to Him for Financial Support and Advice (Islamabad 04450)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Haqqani History: Bin Ladin's Advocate Inside the Taliban
note: [Confidential] Sources say Jalaluddin Haqqani is an important advocate for Osama bin Laden within the Taliban administration. Bin Laden appears to operate largely free of Taliban control and to be protected by Taliban elements. His growing autonomy is attributed to the strength of supporters such as Haqqani, who are ideologically close to him and have argued for reducing controls on him.

title: Afghanistan: [Excised] Criticizes GOP's Afghan Policy; Says It Is Letting Policy Drift
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] Embassy talks with a source who appears to be former Interior Minister Nasrullah Babar on Pakistan's Afghan policy and border control. Babar notes strengthening Pashtun ties and says he supported deploying ISI officers from the Kabul embassy and from Herat, Kandahar and Jalalabad consulates to advise the Taliban while letting the GOP monitor the ISI.

title: Bad News on Pak Afghan Policy: GOP Support for the Taliban Appears to be Getting Stronger
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] Sourced to journalist Ahmed Rashid and UN adviser Arnie Schifferdecker, shows Pakistan agreed to give the Taliban 300 million rupees (about $6.5 million), at 50 million rupees monthly, to pay Taliban officials and commanders. Pakistani Afghan desk officer Ayyaz Wazir called it humanitarian assistance. Comment discusses the effect of the May 1998 nuclear tests and India-Pakistan tension.

title: Afghanistan: In July 2 Meeting, [Excised] Defends Discriminatory Edicts on Women and Girls, and Controls on NGO's
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
note: [Confidential] Embassy official Joe Novak meets a source who appears to be Taliban official Abdul Mujahid, urging withdrawal of edicts discriminating against women and controlling NGOs. Mujahid confirms the GOP 300 million rupee commitment and smiles when told it pays Taliban salaries. He says the Taliban keep tight control of bin Laden and that forcing him out is implausible given Mullah Omar's commitment to him.

title: In Bilateral Focussed on Afghanistan, GOP Reviews Pak/Iran Effort; A/S Inderfurth Expresses U.S. Concerns About the Taliban (Islama 05535)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] A/S Karl Inderfurth meets Pakistani Foreign Minister Shamshad Ahmed on joint Pakistan/Iran talks and Pakistan's role. Ahmed denies providing anything but oil and wheat to the Taliban and says similar help went to the northern factions.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Set to Shift "Diplomatic" Personnel in New York, Riyadh, and Islamabad (Islama 05710)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] The Taliban are moving their "diplomatic" personnel; Taliban have official ties only with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Discusses Abdul Wahab, Abdul Hakim Mujahid and Syed-ur Rahman Haqqani, one of the few non-Pashtun Taliban, educated in a Pakistani madrassa. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Evidence Not There to Prove Assertions that Pak Troops Have Been Deployed to Assist Taliban in the North (Islama 005964)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] No evidence supports claims that Pakistani troops took part in Taliban victories, though Pakistani military advisers may have trained fighters. An estimated 20-40 percent of Taliban soldiers are Pakistani nationals. Bin Laden is mentioned as supporting pro-Taliban Arab fighters from an office in Herat.

title: Bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam - An Update
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA briefing materials giving an update on the Nairobi and Dar es Salaam embassy bombings. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 4, Endnote 37.

title: Executive Order 13099, Prohibiting Transactions With Terrorists Who Threaten to Disrupt the Middle East Peace Process
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
note: [Unclassified] Issued after the embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania, on the day of the retaliatory strikes in Afghanistan and Sudan. It amends EO 12947 to add Usama bin Ladin, the Al-Qaida organization and two other individuals to the list of those whose assets are blocked, and drops 'organizations' from the list heading. Federal Register Vol. 63, No. 164.

title: TFXX01: Afghanistan: Reaction to U.S. Strikes Follows Predicable Lines: Taliban Angry, Their Opponents Support U.S.
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Secret] After the air strikes, Mullah Omar declares the Taliban will never hand over bin Laden. Hamid Karzai tells the Department that bin Laden is on the move and that several Taliban officials are unhappy with Omar for bringing the U.S. against Afghanistan. Overall the strikes have not produced an anti-American reaction in Afghanistan; many Afghans see bin Laden as more of a burden than a blessing.

title: Pakistan: Reaction to Afghanistan Strikes
authors: U.S. Department of State (Assistant Secretary for South Asian Affairs Karl F. Inderfurth to the Secretary of State)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan's Bin Laden Policy
note: [Confidential] Information memorandum written the day after U.S. missile strikes in Afghanistan and Sudan. Clinton calls Nawaz Sharif; the conversation is cordial, but Islamabad decides to take a hard line against the strikes. Inderfurth does not expect the negative reaction to subside. The Sharif government operates amid conspiracy theories and cannot condemn bin Laden without alienating religious parties. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban's Mullah Omar's 8/22 Contact with State Department (State 154712)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Confidential (NODIS)] Mullah Omar phones State two days after the 20 Aug 1998 missile strikes and speaks with Michael Malinowski, director for Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh affairs. It appears to be his only direct contact with a U.S. official. He suggests Clinton resign, predicts more attacks, demands proof of bin Laden's involvement in the Africa bombings, and criticizes the U.S. military presence in Saudi Arabia. Malinowski finds him 'in no way threatening'. Excised.

title: Message to the Taliban on Bin Laden (State 154713)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] Apparent response to Mullah Omar's request for evidence. It outlines the justification for the U.S. strikes, the case against bin Laden, and grounds for his expulsion. It cites 'reliable intelligence' that the bin Laden network sought weapons of mass destruction, including chemical weapons, and had tried to blow up U.S. airliners in the Pacific.

title: TFX01: SITREP 5: Pakistan/Afghanistan Reaction to U.S. Air Strikes
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Confidential] Pakistan remains largely calm after the August 20 strikes. A Pakistani newspaper claims Mullah Omar is displeased with bin Laden for threatening retaliation and for undermining his control of Afghanistan's international relations. Excised.

title: SITREP 6: Pakistan/Afghanistan Reaction to U.S. Strikes (Islama 06433)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Confidential] SITREP on reactions to the 20 Aug strikes. Gen. Joseph Ralston was in Islamabad during the strikes, and Pakistani officials were outraged at the airspace violation. The Taliban called the Khost strikes appalling and hardened their stance on extraditing bin Laden. Mullahs Zakiri and Shinwari issued a fatwa requiring Muslims to protect bin Laden. Excised.

title: SITREP 7: Pakistan/Afghanistan Reaction to U.S. Strikes (Islama 06448)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Confidential] The Pakistani military press office clarifies Gen. Ralston's presence in Islamabad on the night of the strikes. The Taliban received the U.S. letter with evidence against bin Laden but called it 'too general' to warrant extradition, and are 'not in favor' of talks with the U.S. after the missile strikes. Excised.

title: Bin Ladin's Jihad: Political Context
authors: U.S. Department of State, Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Confidential] Intelligence assessment of the political context behind bin Laden's terrorism. It concludes his extremism has found fertile ground in the Arab world, where perceptions of U.S. policies breed feelings of injustice and victimization. Few Arabs endorse his terrorism but many share some of his political sentiments.

title: Afghanistan: Taleban External Ambitions
authors: U.S. Department of State, Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Secret] Despite limited capacity, signs including Mullah Omar's statements after the embassy bombings indicate a broadening of Taliban goals. Under bin Laden's influence the Taliban may expand beyond Afghanistan. Taliban-like movements in Pakistan are already feeling its influence, and Iran fears Sunni cross-border subversion.

title: Terrorism: U.S. Response to Bombings in Kenya and Tanzania: A New Policy Direction?
authors: Raphael F. Perl, Congressional Research Service
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
note: [Unclassified] After the August 1998 embassy bombings, the U.S. struck training bases and infrastructure in Afghanistan used by groups affiliated with Usama bin Ladin and a plant in Sudan. The report says these were the first unreservedly acknowledged preemptive strikes on a terrorist network. It examines whether this is a new policy direction and the issues raised: preparedness, loss of life and civil liberties.

title: Talking Points Regarding Usama Bin Ladin for the DCI's 2 September 1998 SSCI Briefing
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA talking points for the DCI's 2 September 1998 briefing to the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 102.

title: Afghanistan: Reported Activities of Extremist Arabs and Pakistanis Since August 20 U.S. Strike on Khost Terrorist Camps
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Confidential] Tracks Arabs and Pakistanis expelled from Khost. Bin Laden is keeping a low profile, probably in Kandahar, where he has stayed at Mullah Omar's residence and is thought to have been ordered to stay close to Omar; many of his followers are moving to Kabul. The strikes reportedly killed about 20 Pakistanis and 15 Arabs. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Demarche to Taliban on New Bin Laden Threat (Islama 06863)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret] Taliban UN envoy Abdul Hakim Mujahid says Mullah Omar is the main reason bin Laden still has sanctuary, that 80% of Taliban officials (including Mullah Mohammad Rabbani) oppose it, and that few Afghans favor his presence. He cites a shared dislike of Iran. The U.S. official asks the Taliban to protect Shiites and the Buddha statues in Bamiyan.

title: [Title Excised]. Terrorism: Incorporation of Ayman Zawahiri's al-Jihad Organization into Usama Bin Ladin's al-Qa'ida; Recent Activities of Egyptian Associates of al-Qa'ida
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA intelligence report on the incorporation of Zawahiri's al-Jihad organization into bin Laden's al-Qa'ida and on recent activities of al-Qa'ida's Egyptian associates. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 2, Endnote 82.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Convene Ulema, Iran and Bin Ladin on the Agenda
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] The upcoming Taliban Ulema will discuss Iran and Bin Laden's presence in Afghanistan. The source sees a divide in Taliban ranks but expects the Ulema to reiterate Mullah Omar's position that Bin Laden is a guest and not proven involved in any bombings.

title: Afghanistan: Tensions Reportedly Mount Within Taliban as Ties With Saudi Arabia Deteriorate Over Bin Ladin (Islama 07242)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Secret] Covers the Taliban's refusal to surrender bin Laden and Saudi Arabia's failed attempts to negotiate his expulsion. Ambassador Milam notes that if Pakistan, the Taliban's closest supporter, backs Saudi Arabia, pressure may become unbearable, but Pakistan had not made its position clear.

title: Message to Mullah Omar (State 181837)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] Contains Mullah Omar's letter faxed to U.S. officials on 24 Sept 1998, which says bin Laden is 'just an excuse made by the U.S.', and the State Department reply. The reply uses 'with us or against us' language, saying those who harbor terrorists must accept responsibility for their actions.

title: Pakistan: Ambassador Raises bin Laden with Foreign Secretary Shamshad Ahmed (Islama 07510)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret] Ambassador William Milam tells Pakistan's Foreign Secretary that, despite other sticking points such as the status of women, the presence of bin Laden and his organization in Afghanistan is the one issue with no flexibility. He asks for Pakistan's help, stressing that U.S. patience is thin and that it needs a settlement in days rather than weeks. Excised.

title: Usama Bin Ladin: GOP Official - Claiming Taliban Want to Get Rid of Bin Ladin - Reviews Three Options for Dealing With Him (Islama 07553)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] A Pakistani official tells Ambassador Milam the Taliban want to rid themselves of bin Laden and lists three options. He emphasizes option two, in which the U.S. would purchase bin Laden from the Taliban for a large sum. The cable also notes Taliban claims that expelling him would get them overthrown because of Pashtun tribal custom. Excised.

title: Usama Bin Laden: High-Level Taliban Official Gives the Standard Line on Bin Laden With a Couple of Nuances, In October 11 Meeting With Ambassador (Islama 07665)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] Milam meets Taliban Foreign Minister Maulawi Wakil Ahmed, the first meeting with a major Taliban official since the missile strikes. The Taliban call bin Laden a 'serious problem' but repeat that the Afghan people would overthrow them if they handed him over. Wakil asks about his treatment in Saudi Arabia and exaggerates that the previous regime invited bin Laden and the Saudis told the Taliban to keep him. Excised.

title: Usama bin Ladin: Coordinating our Efforts and Sharpening our Message on bin Ladin (Islama 07841)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret] Discusses coordinating with UN efforts and pressing Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and the Taliban to cooperate on bin Laden. It reiterates that the U.S. reserves the right to take military action and will hold the Taliban responsible. It notes the need for pressure before the Khost strikes become 'old news' and calls Saudi Arabia the 'cornerstone' of efforts. Excised.

title: Usama bin Ladin: Coordinating Our Efforts and Sharpening Our Message on Bin Ladin
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Secret] Recommends working closely with the Saudis, the cornerstone of U.S. efforts, and sharpening the message to Pakistan and the Taliban on expelling bin Laden. It suggests Saudi pressure on Taliban trade via the UAE, says Pakistan's lack of support must change, and notes Mullah Omar appears strongly committed to bin Laden. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Leader Mullah Omar: Intimations of Radical Pan-Islamic Thinking?
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Secret] The Department questions its assumption that Mullah Omar has only Afghan nationalist goals. His statements suggest growing sympathy for pan-Islamic movements such as al-Qaeda, possibly through bin Laden's influence. Omar is described as poorly educated and unsure of foreign affairs, and the Taliban might never expel bin Laden. Excised.

title: Talking Points (undated, likely November 1998)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan's Bin Laden Policy
note: [Secret/NODIS] State Department talking points say the U.S. has pressed the Taliban directly and through Pakistan to expel bin Laden, without success. The issue is to be raised at the December 2, 1998 Clinton-Sharif meeting. The Taliban will not surrender him, partly because of his close ties to Mullah Omar, and Pakistan has not been supportive. The time for a diplomatic solution may be running out. Excised.

title: Usama bin Ladin: Taliban Announce Cut-Off Date for Receipt of Evidence; GOP Official Says Taliban Growing More Intransigent (Islama 08369)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret] Two sources, including a Pakistani government official, say the Taliban are growing more inflexible on extraditing bin Laden. They attribute this to press reports that the Saudi Interior Minister exonerated bin Laden over Khobar Towers and Riyadh, and to the lack of U.S. evidence. The Taliban set a 20 Nov 1998 cut-off date for evidence to their Supreme Court. Excised.

title: Afghanistan: Message to Taliban on Usama Bin Laden (State 210367)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] Ambassador Milam is asked to tell the Taliban that the U.S. has now provided greater evidence of bin Laden's terrorist activities and that the Taliban will be held responsible for any terrorist action he undertakes. Excised.

title: Usama Bin Ladin: Message Delivered to Taliban Representative (State 210511)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] Low-level Taliban official Syedur Rahman Haqqani says bin Laden 'is totally under control' and should not be held responsible for those he trained (over 20,000 trained for jihad). He says the Saudi attitude is unclear and that the Taliban welcome proof linking bin Laden to terrorism. Excised.

title: Further Options Available Against Usama Bin Ladin
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA summary report on further options against bin Laden. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 121.

title: Your Meeting on Usama bin Laden (Talking Points)
authors: Assistant Secretary Karl F. Inderfurth to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Department of State
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Secret/NODIS] Talking points noting that negotiations with the Taliban and Pakistan on bin Laden have failed and his network still threatens American lives. The December meeting with Nawaz Sharif is an opportunity to press the message. The Taliban brush-off of the indictment may signal a move from tolerance to more active support. Excised.

title: Your Meeting on Usama bin Laden
authors: Assistant Secretary Karl F. Inderfurth to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Department of State
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Secret] Briefing memorandum outlining key points on bin Laden and how to persuade the Taliban to expel him to a country where he can be brought to justice. The U.S. holds the Taliban responsible, but efforts to get him expelled have been frustrated by his ties to Mullah Omar. Excised.

title: [Excised] Options for Attacking the Usama Bin Ladin Problem
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA talking points on options for attacking the bin Laden problem. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 121.

title: Osama bin Laden: Taliban Spokesman Seeks New Proposal for Resolving bin Laden Problem (State 220495)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret] After the Taliban Supreme Court finds insufficient evidence against bin Laden, Wakil Ahmed tells DCM Alan Eastham that Kandahar does not consider the matter resolved and that Saudi Arabia holds the key. Eastham corrects Wakil's claim that bin Laden was U.S.-supported, saying the U.S. had never heard his name in that period. Wakil also says Saddam Hussein was the root cause of the problems. Excised.

title: Osama bin Laden: Taliban Spokesman Seeks New Proposal for Resolving bin Laden Problem
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Secret] Taliban spokesman Wakil Ahmed says the Taliban understand the U.S. wants bin Laden expelled, and that Kandahar is still seeking a way to resolve the issue. He says that had Kandahar been able to retaliate with similar strikes against Washington, it would have. He says a Saudi "pride" blocked an authentic proposal, and suggests the U.S. could kill bin Laden, though he asks that it not. Excised.

title: [Title Excised] Planning by Usama Bin Ladin to Hijack U.S. Airplane, Successful Circumvention of Security Measures in U.S. Airport
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Raw intelligence report that became the basis for the 4 Dec 1998 President's Daily Brief. Says bin Laden planned new operations against U.S. targets, the hijack plan was proceeding well, and two operatives from the U.S. team evaded security in a trial run at a New York airport. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 112.

title: Bin Ladin Preparing to Hijack US Aircraft and Other Attacks
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA intelligence report on bin Laden preparing to hijack US aircraft and carry out other attacks. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 112.

title: Afghanistan: Longstanding Tensions Between Taliban Leader Omar and Deputy Leader Rabbani Said To Be On Increase (Islama 09020)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Growing tensions between Omar and Rabbani, particularly over protecting bin Laden: Omar rejects expulsion or extradition while Rabbani wants the matter settled before further isolation. An open break is unlikely. Saudi Arabia denied Mullah Rabbani a visa but granted one to Burhanuddin Rabbani. Excised.

title: Usama bin Ladin: Pakistan Seems to Be Leaning Against Being Helpful (Islamabad 09215)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan's Bin Laden Policy
note: [Secret] After the Clinton-Sharif meeting, the Embassy concludes the Government of Pakistan is not disposed to be especially helpful on bin Ladin. Pakistani sources say bin Ladin is a problem the U.S. has with the Taliban, not with Pakistan. It cites a journalist with ISI connections saying Pakistan wants nothing to do with the anti-Osama crusade. The Embassy will keep trying but calls it an uphill slog. Excised.

title: [Title Excised] Possible Arrest of Two Persons Involved in Plan to Hijack U.S. Airplane in the United States
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA intelligence report on the possible arrest of two persons involved in the plan to hijack a U.S. airplane in the United States. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 113.

title: Usama bin Ladin: Charge Reiterates U.S. Concern to Key Taliban Official, Who Sticks to Well-Known Taliban Positions (Islama 09222)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret] Wakil Ahmed tells Eastham he discussed U.S. concerns with Mullah Omar and that the Taliban still consider bin Laden innocent. He says the Taliban remain deeply upset over the Khost strikes and calls the U.S. 'murderers of Afghans'.

title: Re: urgent re ubl
authors: CIA (from [Excised], likely Gary Schroen, to Michael F. Scheuer)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA email note for Michael F. Scheuer from [Excised]. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report as "[Gary] Schroen to Mike" (Chapter 4, Endnotes 117, 119).

title: Afghanistan: Bio-Data on Maulawi Abdul Wahab, Taliban Embassy Official in Saudi Arabia (Islama 09278)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Background on the new Taliban representative in Riyadh. His predecessor Maulawi Dilawar was told to leave Saudi Arabia in September 1998 because of the dispute over Usama bin Ladin. Excised.

title: your note
authors: CIA (Michael F. Scheuer to [Excised], likely Gary Schroen)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA email note from Michael F. Scheuer to [Excised]. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report as "Mike to [Gary] Schroen" (Chapter 4, Endnote 119).

title: CIA Biography, Mohammad Omar
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
note: [Unclassified] CIA document released to the media in 1998. It covers the birth, education and professional career of the Taliban leader, including time as a subcommander of a faction of the Afghan resistance.

title: Usama bin Ladin: Saudi Government Reportedly Turning the Screws on the Taliban on Visas; Haj May be Affected
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
note: [Confidential] In response to Taliban intransigence on surrendering bin Laden, Saudi Arabia is restricting Afghan travel to the holy sites and reportedly barred Ariana from flying between Kabul or Kandahar and Jeddah. The Taliban would suffer great embarrassment if the Saudi government does not accept their Haj list. Excised.

title: [Excised] Timeframe for Completion of Hijacking Operation [Excised]
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA intelligence report on the timeframe for completion of the hijacking operation. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 113.

title: Usama Bin Ladin: Bin Ladin Uses Recent Interviews to Assert Right to WMD, and to Threaten U.S. and U.K Over Iraq (Islama 09420)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] Reports two bin Laden interviews since the August strikes. He asserts a right to use WMD and urges Muslims to kill U.S., British and Israeli civilians, citing Iraq strikes. He denies involvement in the Africa bombings, alleges a Saudi hit squad, and describes mutual respect with the Taliban.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban "Threat Warning" (Islama 09424)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] The Taliban send an unspecific message that terrorists backed by Ahmed Shah Massoud and Iranian intelligence are plotting against the U.S. State believes the motives are probably political, since Massoud and Iran are among the Taliban's most powerful enemies.

title: Usama Bin Ladin: Charge Underscores U.S. Concerns on Interviews; Taliban Envoy Says Bin Ladin Hoodwinked Them and it Will Not Happen Again (Islama 09488)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
note: [Secret (NODIS)] Taliban representative Syedur Rahman Haqqani says the Taliban allowed bin Laden to be interviewed so he could renounce terrorism, but he instead reiterated his commitment to attacking Americans and his right to use WMD. Haqqani promises no more interviews or terrorist activity, and says being 'tricked' did not change bin Laden's status as a guest.

title: Afghanistan: The Taliban's Decision-Making Process and Leadership Structure (Islama 09531)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Updates the 1997 review: Omar is stronger than ever and enforces policy via the Ministry to Propagate Virtue and Prevent Vice. The Inner and Outer shuras are weakening while the Ulema Shura gains influence. Omar, perhaps under bin Ladin's influence, may be more sympathetic to pan-Islamism. Taliban decision-making remains opaque. Excised.

title: Strains Surface Between Taliban and Bin Ladin
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA analytic report, undated. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report as January 1999 (p. 342; Chapter 11, Endnote 5).

title: Ambassador Reviews Again GOP Policy on Afghanistan (Islamabad 00138)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan's Bin Laden Policy
note: [Secret] Heavily excised account of Ambassador William Milam's meeting with Foreign Minister Sartaj Aziz. The U.S. urged the GOP to get active in convincing the Taliban to expel Usama bin Ladin and to change its pro-Taliban policies. Aziz listened carefully but his response contained little that was new.

title: [Title Excised], Claim that Bin Ladin Postponed Hijacking
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA intelligence report on a claim that bin Laden postponed the hijacking. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 113.

title: How Bin Ladin Commands a Global Terrorist Network (99-40003)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CTC intelligence report 99-40003 on how bin Laden commands a global terrorist network. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 5, Endnote 118 and Chapter 6, Endnote 86.

title: [Excised] Talking Points: CIA Operations Against Usama Bin Ladin
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA talking points on CIA operations against bin Laden. Cited in 9/11 Commission Report Chapter 4, Endnote 157.

title: Afghanistan: Taliban Seem to Have Less Funds and Supplies This Year, But the Problem Does Not Appear to be that Acute (Islama 01320)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Confidential] Under post-nuclear-test sanctions Pakistan reduced Taliban aid, though it still wrote a check of about a million dollars every couple of months. Saudi private donations fell, bin Laden gave the Taliban some money, and Masoud remains well funded by Iran, Russia, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.

publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Osama Bin Laden File
note: The 6 August 2001 President's Daily Brief, marked 'For the President Only'. It says FBI information indicates patterns of suspicious activity consistent with preparations for hijackings or other attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York. Condoleezza Rice told the 9-11 Commission it was not a real warning. (Matched by page context; no anchor text.)

title: Bin Ladin Determined to Strike in US
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: President's Daily Brief. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 8, Endnote 38; reprinted on p. 261 of the Report.

title: Terrorism: Bin Ladin Determined to Strike in the US
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Senior Executive Intelligence Brief. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 8, Endnote 38; Chapter 11, Endnote 5; p. 342.

title: Re: Khalid Al-Mihdhar
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA email memorandum cited in the 9/11 Commission Report as "Mary to John." Source: Chapter 8, Endnote 106.

title: DCI Update Terrorist Threat Review
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA DCI update on the terrorist threat. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 8, Endnote 103.

title: Terrorism: Sanitized Version of Threat Report
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA intelligence report. As of late August 2001, indications that an al-Qaeda-associated individual was considering terrorist operations in the US; no further information on timing or targets. Source: Chapter 8, Endnote 39.

title: Staffdel Focuses on Afghanistan at MFA (Islamabad 04780)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Sensitive But Unclassified] Less than two weeks before 9/11, U.S. congressional staff meet Pakistani Foreign Ministry officials. The Pakistanis say they "don't support, but inter-act with the Taliban" and deny that ISI or the government arms the Taliban. They recommend engagement, saying Taliban obscurantism, not Pashtun tribalism, drives the war, and suggest corrupting the Taliban with aid and a reborn economy.

title: Terrorism: Near Eastern Groups and State Sponsors, 2001
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
note: [Unclassified] CRS study published September 10, 2001. It profiles many terrorist groups (radical Islamic groups including Al-Qaida, radical Jewish, leftwing and nationalist groups) and state sponsorship by Iran, Syria, Libya, Sudan and Iraq. It also covers countering terrorism in the region. The summary notes a decline in state sponsorship and a rise in the threat from Usama bin Ladin's independent network.

title: Musharraf [EXCISED] (Islamabad 05087)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret - Noforn] Two days after 9/11, Ambassador Wendy Chamberlin bluntly tells Musharraf that the attacks changed the fundamentals of the debate. There was absolutely no inclination in Washington to enter into a dialogue with the Taliban, and the time for dialogue ended September 11. She says the Taliban are harboring the terrorists responsible for the attacks.

title: Action Plan as of 9/13/2001 7:55:51am
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Two days after 9/11, State creates an action plan documenting U.S. government activities so far and an immediate to-do list. It includes high-level meetings with Pakistani officials, including ISI Director Mahmoud Ahmed, and diplomatic approaches to Russia, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Georgia, Sudan, China and Indonesia.

title: Musharraf: We Are With You in Your Action Plan in Afghanistan (Islamabad 05087)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret/Noforn] Ambassador Wendy Chamberlin bluntly tells Musharraf that 9/11 changed the fundamentals of the Afghanistan-Pakistan debate, that there is no inclination to dialogue with the Taliban, and that the Taliban are harboring the terrorists responsible. A less-redacted version of a document previously posted in 2010.

title: Deputy Secretary Armitage's Meeting with Pakistan Intel Chief Mahmud: You're Either With Us or You're Not (State 157813) [Version 1]
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Armitage meets ISI Chief Mahmoud Ahmed the day after 9/11 and presents a 'stark choice': Pakistan must stand with the U.S. or against it, with 'no grey.' Mahmud pledges 'unqualified support' and denies Pakistan was ever 'in bed' with those threatening U.S. interests, which conflicts with U.S. intelligence on Pakistani support for the Taliban. Version 1 contains more released text.

title: Deputy Secretary Armitage's Meeting with Pakistan Intel Chief Mahmud: You're Either With Us or You're Not (State 157813) [Version 2]
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Second, differently redacted release of the Armitage-Mahmud meeting cable. It includes a few sections absent from Version 1, such as paragraph 10, noting that Mahmud's CIA colleagues would talk with him soon and that he had been in touch with Langley after the attacks.

title: Talking Points
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Talking points for Secretary Powell drafted two days after 9/11. Objectives include eliminating bin Laden's al-Qaida. Focus is on regional support from Pakistan, India and Bangladesh and cooperation with Saudi Arabia and Egypt; the U.S. will also probe Iran's ability to work against the Taliban and bin Laden.

title: Deputy Secretary Armitage's Meeting with General Mahmud: Actions and Support Expected of Pakistan in Fight Against Terrorism (State 158711)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret] On September 13, 2001 Armitage meets ISI chief Mahmoud Ahmed and presents seven demands for Musharraf's approval. They include stopping al-Qaida at the border, blanket overflight and landing rights, territorial access, intelligence sharing, public condemnation of terrorism, cutting off fuel and recruits to the Taliban, and breaking relations with the Taliban if the evidence implicates bin Ladin.

title: Musharraf Accepts The Seven Points (Islamabad 05123)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret] After meeting his military commanders, Musharraf accepts the seven U.S. requests "without conditions," while noting technical issues needing clarification. He asks whether the U.S. mission targets UBL and his supporters or the Taliban as well, urges a prompt economic recovery effort after military action, and says Islamabad wants a friendly government in Kabul.

title: Deputy Secretary Armitage's Meeting with General Mahmud: Actions and Support Expected of Pakistan in Fight Against Terrorism (State 159711)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Armitage again meets ISI Chief Mahmoud Ahmed and lists specific requests for Musharraf's approval: stop al-Qaida operatives at the border, intercept arms shipments, end logistical support for bin Laden, grant overflight and territorial access, share intelligence, cut off fuel and recruits to the Taliban, and break relations with the Taliban if evidence implicates bin Laden. Less redacted than the 2010 version.

title: Gameplan for Polmil Strategy for Pakistan and Afghanistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret/NODIS] Since the attacks show UBL can conduct terrorism under Taliban control, State proposes demands on the Taliban (surrender al-Qaeda associates, provide intelligence, expel terrorists), subtle ways to encourage splits in Taliban leadership, and use of force if the deadline is missed. It stresses coordination with Pakistan, the Central Asian states, Russia and possibly Iran; Pakistan will not send troops into Afghanistan but will give other support.

title: Talking Points for PC 0930 on 14 September 2001
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Unspecified] Powell's talking points for an NSC Principals Committee meeting on the immediate response to 9/11. Objectives: setting the stage for a forceful response, eradicating bin Laden's al-Qaida, and eliminating safehaven for terrorism. Powell notes moderate Arabs are seeing terrorism in a new light, which is key to the coalition.

title: Musharraf Accepts The Seven Points (Islamabad 05123)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] After meeting military commanders, Musharraf accepts the seven U.S. requested actions without conditions, though technical issues need clarification. He asks whether the U.S. aims to strike UBL or the Taliban too, urges a prompt economic recovery effort after any military action, and says Islamabad wants a friendly government in Kabul.

title: Deputy Secretary Armitage-Mamoud Phone Call – September 18, 2001 (State 161279)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Confidential] ISI Director Mahmoud Ahmed flew to Afghanistan on September 17 aboard a U.S. government aircraft to meet Mullah Omar. He relayed three U.S. conditions: hand over UBL, hand over his 13 top lieutenants, and close terrorist training camps. Mahmoud says the Taliban response was not negative on all points and that Afghan Islamic leaders were in deep introspection.

title: Deputy Secretary Armitage-Mamoud Phone Call – September 18, 2001 (State 161279)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Confidential] ISI Director Mahmoud Ahmed travels to Afghanistan on September 17 to meet Mullah Omar and conveys three U.S. conditions: hand over UBL, hand over 13 top lieutenants, and close terrorist training camps. Mahmoud says the Taliban's response was 'not negative on all these points.'

title: Secretary's 13 September 2001 Conversation with Pakistani President Musharraf (State 161371)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Powell's September 13 phone call with Musharraf. Powell says Pakistan has a vital role because of its unique relationship with the Taliban and that 'as one general to another, we need someone on our flank fighting with us.'

title: Mahmud Plans 2nd Mission to Afghanistan (Islamabad 05123)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret] ISI Director Mahmoud tells Ambassador Chamberlin he is returning to Afghanistan to make a last plea to the Taliban. He believes a negotiated solution is preferable and urges her "not to act in anger. Real victory will come in negotiations." He says it is better for the Afghans to deal with bin Laden and warns of warlordism if the Taliban are eliminated. Chamberlin replies that Omar has refused every U.S. demand and the trip cannot delay military planning.

title: Mahmud Plans 2nd Mission to Afghanistan (Islamabad 05337)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] ISI Director Mahmoud tells Ambassador Chamberlin he will make a last-minute plea to the Taliban, preferring a negotiated solution and saying Omar is frightened. He promises full Pakistani support, including for military action. Chamberlin says Omar has refused every U.S. demand and the trip cannot delay military planning.

title: Mahmud on Failed Kandahar Trip (Islamabad 05452)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Confidential] Mahmoud's September 28 two-hour meeting with Taliban Deputy Foreign Minister Jalil ends with no progress; Mullah Omar agreed only to 'think about' proposals. The Ambassador confirms the U.S. will not negotiate with the Taliban.

title: Strategic Thoughts
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Rumsfeld)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Top Secret/Close Hold] Rumsfeld advises President Bush to think beyond al-Qaeda in Afghanistan, favoring equip-and-train efforts with local opposition forces and humanitarian aid over aerial strikes. He argues the war must 'significantly change the world's political map', with new regimes in Afghanistan and another state that supports terrorism.

title: Afghanistan: Al-Qaida Military Contribution to the Taleban
authors: Department of State, Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Newly Published Documents Cast Doubt on Claims Taliban Will Give Up al Qaeda | National Security Archive
note: [Secret] Second review/release of the same October 1, 2001 INR report on al Qaeda's military contribution to the Taliban, including the 055 Brigade. The page notes the other release fully obscured the section on jointly run al Qaeda–Taliban training camps, showing reviewers initially thought release would harm national security.

title: Afghanistan: Al-Qaida Military Contribution to the Taleban
authors: Department of State, Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Newly Published Documents Cast Doubt on Claims Taliban Will Give Up al Qaeda | National Security Archive
note: [Secret] Two-page INR report on the Taliban's growing reliance on bin Laden and al Qaeda for financial and military support against the Northern Alliance. It covers the 55th (055) Brigade of expatriate mujahideen loyal to bin Laden, estimated at 500-2,500 men. One of two releases of the same report; the earlier one fully redacts the section on camps jointly run by al Qaeda and the Taliban.

title: IIR [Excised]/Veteran Afghanistan Traveler's Analysis of Al Qaeda and Taliban Exploitable Weaknesses
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Secret] DIA report on the status of the Taliban and al-Qaeda and strategy for the coming US-led war, stressing human intelligence. Notes that Bin Laden's al-Qaeda network expanded under the safe sanctuary extended by the Taliban following Pakistan directives, elucidating the ISI connection.

title: IIR [Excised]/Veteran Afghanistan Traveler's Analysis of Al Qaeda and Taliban Military, Political and Cultural Landscape and its Weaknesses
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Secret] Details events in Afghanistan and Pakistan's role in supporting the Taliban. Pakistan groomed weak commanders like Hekmatyar, whose failure led it to introduce the Taliban. Notes Musharraf's troubling position hunting culprits he helped establish, and summarizes al-Qaeda and Pakistani agendas and the death of Masoud.

title: Strategic Guidance for the Campaign Against Terrorism
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Top Secret] Expansive strategic guidance to DoD for developing campaign plans, specifying threats (terrorist organizations, harboring states including the Taliban and Iraq Baathist Party, WMD proliferation), objectives, means, concepts and campaign elements.

title: [Title Excised]
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Confidential] Reflecting Pakistan's post-9/11 policy change, a DIA source discusses Pakistan and Musharraf's support for the fight against terrorism. Assisting the US serves Pakistan's self-interest and Pakistan wants recognition and assistance for its commitment.

title: Message to Taliban (State 175415)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret/Nodis/Eyes Only] The U.S. asks ISI chief Mahmoud or Musharraf to deliver a message to the Taliban: hand over al-Qaida leaders or face a devastating response, Taliban leaders will be held personally responsible, and 'every pillar of the Taliban regime will be destroyed.'

title: Prospects for Northern Alliance Forces to Seize Kabul
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret/Noforn/X1] Compares Taliban and Northern Alliance strength around Kabul. The Taliban Kabul Central Corps has about 130 tanks and 7,000 soldiers against Fahim Khan's roughly 10,000 troops. The Alliance is unlikely to seize Kabul unaided, but Russian arms deliveries via Tajikistan may change the balance. The Alliance took Kabul on November 13, 2001.

title: Strategy / U.S. Strategy in Afghanistan (Rumsfeld to Feith, with NSC attachment)
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Rumsfeld) / National Security Council
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret/Close Hold/Draft for Discussion] NSC outlines U.S. strategy five weeks after 9/11: destroy al-Qaeda and the Taliban without committing to post-Taliban military involvement, use any Afghan tribes and factions, insert CIA teams and special forces in the north and south, and engage Pakistan, Iran and Russia. Includes a handwritten Rumsfeld note.

title: Afghanistan (Rumsfeld to General Myers)
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Rumsfeld)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Rumsfeld expresses frustration at the Defense Department's near total dependence on the CIA, which must go into Afghanistan first to prepare the way for DoD.

title: Discussions w/CENTCOM re: Sy Hersh Article
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Rumsfeld)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Rumsfeld is concerned by Hersh's report that CENTCOM failed to fire on a convoy thought to carry Mullah Omar. He had told Franks to hit it if anyone wiggled, and says he has a high tolerance for possible error in strikes.

title: Rumsfeld snowflake to Douglas Feith, "Strategy," with Attachment "U.S. Strategy in Afghanistan" (NSC, Oct 16, 2001)
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Donald Rumsfeld); attachment by National Security Council
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan 20/20: The 20-Year War in 20 Documents | National Security Archive
note: [Secret] Foundational document for the first phase of U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, approved by the NSC on Oct 16, 2001, with Rumsfeld's handwritten edits and an Oct 30 cover note to Feith. It stresses destroying al-Qaeda and the Taliban, using any and all Afghan tribes and factions, inserting CIA teams and special forces, and avoiding commitment to post-Taliban military involvement. Diplomacy with Pakistan, Iran and Russia is emphasized, while UN diplomacy is limited.

title: Your Meeting with Pakistani President Musharraf (Memorandum for the President)
authors: Secretary of State Colin Powell to President George W. Bush (Department of State)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret] Powell highlights changes in U.S.-Pakistan relations since 9/11, including cooperation on counterterrorism, nonproliferation, protection of Pakistani nuclear assets and economic development. Musharraf allied with the U.S. at considerable political risk, abandoning the Taliban and freezing terrorist assets. He is pressing for a future Afghan government supportive of Pakistan's interests and fears the Northern Alliance will occupy Kabul.

title: Your Meeting with Pakistani President Musharraf
authors: U.S. Department of State (Secretary Powell to President Bush)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Powell highlights changes in U.S.-Pakistan relations since 9/11: cooperation on counterterrorism, nuclear nonproliferation and economic development. Musharraf has abandoned the Taliban at political risk and is concerned the Northern Alliance will occupy Kabul. Previously released in 2010.

title: Pakistan - Poll Shows Strong and Growing Public Support for Taleban
authors: Carl W. Ford Jr., Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, to Secretary Powell
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
note: [Unclassified] A post-9/11 INR poll shows the Pakistani public more pro-Taliban than before September 11, even as the Musharraf government distances Pakistan from its longstanding Taliban alliance.

title: IIR Taliban Leadership, Part 1 – Mullah Omar and the Council of Ministers
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Confidential] Updated biographical summaries of Taliban members. Notes one of Omar's sons was reportedly killed in October 2001 air strikes, Mullah Hassan Akhund's rise to Vice President of the Council of Ministers, and Rabbani's death from cancer in April 2001. Excised.

title: Scene-Setter for the Visit of Senators Levin and Warner (Islamabad 06322)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret] Prepares Senators Levin and Warner for their Pakistan visit. Pakistan's cooperation against al-Qaida and the Taliban has been unstinting, and Musharraf has held firm by placing five Islamist leaders under house arrest and changing military leadership (ISI's Mahmoud replaced by Ehsan ul Haq). Sanctions are lifted and aid is rising, but Pakistan remains wary of the Northern Alliance and wants Kabul demilitarized under UN or OIC control.

title: IIR [Excised]/The Assassination of Massoud Related to 11 September 2001 Attack
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Secret] DIA assesses the link between the assassination of Northern Alliance Commander Ahmad Shah Masoud and the 9/11 attacks. Masoud had apparently gained limited knowledge of Bin Ladin's and al-Qaida's intentions to attack the US on a scale larger than the 1998 embassy bombings.

title: Terrorism: Extremists Planning Attacks Against US Interests in Pakistan
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA analytic report on extremists planning attacks against US interests in Pakistan. Source: 9/11 Commission Report, Chapter 2, Endnote 80.

title: 'New Think': Our Long-Term Interests in Pakistan (Islamabad 06522)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret] The embassy urges Washington to keep extensive aid flowing to secure long-term regional interests, since U.S. counterterrorism in Afghanistan depends on Pakistani support. It notes widespread Pakistani mistrust, "we helped you in Afghanistan twenty years ago, and then America walked away." It argues aid is the most effective tool for showing that the U.S. is a long-term partner.

title: Rumsfeld complains to George Tenet about the CIA
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Rumsfeld Lacked Intel on Who The Enemies Were Two Years After Afghanistan Invasion, Newly Published "Snowflakes" Show | National Security Archive
note: Rumsfeld complains to George Tenet about the CIA.

title: IIR [Excised] Pakistani Political, Military Situation, and Terrorism Issues
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
note: [Secret] Discusses the political and military situation in Pakistan, including government stability, armed forces capabilities and terrorism issues in the post-September 11 climate.

title: Identifying Al-Qa'ida's Donors and Fundraisers: A Status Report
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA analytic report on al-Qaeda donors and fundraisers. Source: Chapter 5, Endnotes 116, 117; Chapter 7, Endnote 70.

title: Rumsfeld snowflake to Larry Di Rita, "Weekly Meeting on Afghanistan"
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Donald Rumsfeld)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan 20/20: The 20-Year War in 20 Documents | National Security Archive
note: [Unclassified] After the swift victory over the Taliban, Rumsfeld worried by March 2002 that Afghanistan was 'drifting' and asked for a weekly meeting. The same day, in a public interview, he said there was no point negotiating with Taliban remnants.

title: Weekly meeting on Afghanistan - it is "drifting"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Rumsfeld Lacked Intel on Who The Enemies Were Two Years After Afghanistan Invasion, Newly Published "Snowflakes" Show | National Security Archive
note: Rumsfeld proposes a weekly meeting on Afghanistan, stating that it is "drifting".

title: Rumsfeld snowflake to Doug Feith, "Afghanistan" ("Help!")
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Donald Rumsfeld)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan 20/20: The 20-Year War in 20 Documents | National Security Archive
note: [Secret] Written the day Bush announced nation-building objectives at VMI. Rumsfeld says the U.S. military will never leave Afghanistan unless something provides the stability needed for departure. Copied to Wolfowitz, Myers and Pace.

title: Rumsfeld tells Hank Crumpton to "speak up"
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Rumsfeld Lacked Intel on Who The Enemies Were Two Years After Afghanistan Invasion, Newly Published "Snowflakes" Show | National Security Archive
note: Rumsfeld tells Hank Crumpton to "speak up".

publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
note: [Secret] Update giving names and positions of 75 Taliban officials, compiled to support UNSCR 1267 asset freezes. Describes Mullah Amir Khan Muttaqi as a key figure in the Taliban's ideological projects who led a 1997 UNOCAL-invited delegation to the U.S. Excised.

title: Rumsfeld snowflake to Douglas Feith, "Pakistan" ("Get the Paks to really fight")
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Donald Rumsfeld)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan 20/20: The 20-Year War in 20 Documents | National Security Archive
note: [Unclassified] Rumsfeld suggests getting a chunk of money to ease Musharraf's transition so Pakistan will fight the war on terror. It shows U.S. naivety about Pakistan and its intelligence service playing both sides; Musharraf received about $10 billion in U.S. aid over six years.

title: Al Qaeda Ops Sec
authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Wolfowitz to Rumsfeld)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
note: [Secret] Intelligence community assumes bin Laden is alive because al-Qaeda could not keep his death secret. Wolfowitz disputes this, arguing al-Qaeda communicates effectively without detection, and warns of overreliance on a classified tracking capability ('the drunk looking for keys under the lamppost').

title: Terrorism: Amount of Money It Takes to Keep al-Qa'ida Functioning (PWR080702-05)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA analytic report on the cost of keeping al-Qaeda functioning. Source: Chapter 5, Endnotes 111, 127.

authors: Combined Joint Special Operations Task Force, Coalition Coordination Cell, Kandahar (Roger Pardo-Maurer); cover note by Donald Rumsfeld (Sept 13, 2002)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan 20/20: The 20-Year War in 20 Documents | National Security Archive
note: [Unclassified] Candid, humorous 14-page email by a Green Beret hunting high-value targets in Kandahar. It warns that border provinces still swarm with 'Bad Guys' (Pakistan as a Taliban sanctuary), recommends a Special Forces approach of fighting alongside Afghans, and says Afghanistan is not really a country. Rumsfeld requested a copy in a Sept 13, 2002 snowflake.

publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Rumsfeld Lacked Intel on Who The Enemies Were Two Years After Afghanistan Invasion, Newly Published "Snowflakes" Show | National Security Archive
note: Rumsfeld sends handwritten notes from an interview with a detainee to Feith.

authors: CIA / Director of Central Intelligence (Joint Inquiry Committee)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: Written statement of the DCI before the Joint Inquiry Committee. Source: Chapter 4, Endnote 103; Chapter 6, Endnote 54; Chapter 8, Endnote 60.

title: S/P Ambassador Haass' Call on [Excised] (Islamabad 09489)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
note: [Secret] Richard Haass meets an unnamed Pakistani military official on October 31, 2002. The official claims there are no al-Qaeda safe havens in Pakistan and that al-Qaeda's tribal-area presence is limited to transit. Haass says al-Qaeda's core is in Pakistan and the threat is as large as on September 10. The official describes FATA's maliks-versus-mullahs conflict and the former "no-go areas" opened briefly after Tora Bora when tribes were overawed by U.S. firepower; "that window [is] closed."

title: Saudi Based Financial Support for Terrorist Organizations (CTC 2002-40117CH)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA analytic report on Saudi-based financial support for terrorist organizations. Source: Chapter 2, Endnote 77.

publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified

authors: Donald Rumsfeld, Secretary of Defense (to Craddock and Haynes)
publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Rumsfeld Lacked Intel on Who The Enemies Were Two Years After Afghanistan Invasion, Newly Published "Snowflakes" Show | National Security Archive

publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA analytic report on al-Qaeda in Sudan 1992-96. Source: Chapter 2, Endnote 30.

publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified
note: CIA intelligence report on al-Qaeda operative Tawfiq bin Attash in Los Angeles in summer 2000 and his association with U.S.-based extremists. Source: Chapter 7, Endnote 9.

title: 11 September: The Plot and the Plotters (CTC 2003-40044HC)
